def: A fluency activity in which a learner gives the same talk three times to different listeners in four, three and then two minutes, so that repetition and time pressure make speech smoother (Nation 1989).

A planning framework for CLIL that asks teachers to integrate content, communication, cognition and culture in each unit (Coyle, Hood and Marsh 2010); for example, a science lesson on the water cycle also plans its language and thinking demands.

The vocabulary, grammar and text structures used in school subjects and study, such as defining, comparing and explaining, as distinct from everyday conversational language; many learners need explicit support to master it.
The features of pronunciation that identify where a speaker comes from or which group they belong to; every speaker has an accent, and an Indian accent is no barrier to being understood.

How strongly a listener perceives a speaker’s pronunciation as differing from a reference variety; research shows that a noticeable accent is often fully intelligible, so accentedness and comprehensibility are separate judgements.

A planning tool that surveys learners’ access to devices, internet, time and study space, groups them by level of access, and provides a version of each outside-class task for every group, so no one is excluded.

The degree to which a lesson, material or test can be used by all learners, including those with sensory, physical or learning differences, through choices such as clear print, spoken instructions and flexible seating.

(1) An adjustment to how a learner accesses a task or test, such as extra time or enlarged print, which changes the route but not the destination. (2) In ELF talk, adjusting one’s speech to be understood by a listener.

The extent to which a learner’s language is free from errors in grammar, vocabulary and pronunciation; one of the three dimensions of performance, with complexity and fluency, that teachers balance in task design.

Small-scale, systematic enquiry by teachers into a problem in their own classroom, moving through cycles of planning, acting, observing and reflecting; for example, testing whether a new seating plan increases pair talk.

Digital instruction in which software adjusts the content, difficulty or pace of tasks according to each learner’s responses; its claims should be checked against independent evidence before a school adopts it.

Learning needs beyond those of most classmates, arising for example from dyslexia, attention difficulties or sensory impairment; changes that help these learners, such as clear routines and uncluttered worksheets, usually help the whole class.

The learning of a second language while the first language continues to be valued and developed, so that the learner gains a language rather than replacing one; for example, adding English to Kannada rather than substituting it.

A professional practice in which an advisor helps learners reflect on and direct their own learning through dialogue, using techniques of listening, questioning and restating rather than instruction (Mynard and Carson 2012).
Emotional and attitudinal influences on learning, such as anxiety, motivation, self-confidence and attitudes to the language, which can make learners more or less willing to take part and take risks.
Krashen’s (1982) metaphor for emotional states such as anxiety or low confidence that block input from being acquired; a relaxed, supportive classroom is said to lower the filter.

A meaningful element attached to a word stem to form a new word or word form, such as the prefix un- in unhappy or the suffix -ness in kindness; teaching common affixes helps learners work out new words.

The age at which a person first moves into an environment where the second language is widely used; research on the critical period uses it as a key variable when comparing learners’ ultimate attainment.

The policies, rules and oversight that decide how artificial intelligence tools are chosen, used and checked in an institution, including questions of transparency, fairness, data privacy and accountability for decisions.

The knowledge and skills needed to use artificial intelligence tools critically and responsibly, including understanding what they can and cannot do, checking their output, and recognizing issues of bias and academic honesty.
Systematic unfairness in the output of an automated system, arising from its training data or design; for example, a scoring engine that marks down features typical of Indian English.

A method of marking in which separate scores are given for different criteria, such as content, organization, vocabulary and grammar, giving more diagnostic information than a single overall (holistic) score.
The theory and practice of teaching adults, which stresses that adults learn best when learning is relevant to their own goals and draws on their experience (Knowles 1980).
In peer feedback, removing writers’ or reviewers’ names so that learners feel freer to give critical comments; it reduces social pressure, though signed praise can help build relationships.
An exam strategy in which learners rule out options they can show to be wrong before choosing an answer to a multiple-choice item; teachers model it by explaining why each wrong option fails.
The difficulties with meaning, form, pronunciation or the task that a teacher predicts learners may have, recorded in a lesson plan together with possible solutions.
A model of teacher education in which trainees first learn theory and research findings and then apply them in the classroom (Wallace 1991); contrast the craft model and the reflective model.
Lortie’s (1975) term for the many hours future teachers spend watching their own teachers as pupils, which shapes their beliefs about teaching before any training begins.
The suitability of a word, phrase or style for its context, purpose and audience; a sentence can be grammatically correct but inappropriate, such as an overly direct request to a principal.
Holliday’s (1994) argument that teaching methods should be fitted to the social and cultural context of each classroom rather than imported unchanged from elsewhere.
A grammatical category showing how an action or state is viewed in time, for example as complete or in progress; English marks progressive aspect (is writing) and perfect aspect (has written).
The explicit qualities against which a piece of work is judged, such as task completion, organization and accuracy; sharing them with learners helps them understand what good work looks like.

A framework in which test developers must justify each link from a test performance to the interpretation of scores, the decisions made and their consequences for test takers (Bachman and Palmer 2010).

In a debate or discussion, a viewpoint that a learner is given to argue rather than one they personally hold; it separates the argument from the arguer and lowers the emotional stakes of disagreement.
In connected speech, the change of a sound so that it becomes more like a neighbouring sound, as when ten boys is pronounced with an m sound at the end of ten.
An agreed, taught cue, such as a raised hand or a clap pattern, that tells learners to stop and listen, helping a teacher regain attention quickly in a large class.
The length of time a learner can concentrate on one activity; it is shorter in young children, so lessons for them need frequent changes of activity and pace.
The loss or decline of language skills over time, usually because a language is no longer used regularly; it can affect a first language as well as a second.
Assessment that asks learners to perform tasks resembling real-world language use, such as writing a letter to a newspaper or conducting an interview, rather than answering isolated test items.
Spoken or written language produced for real communicative purposes rather than for language teaching, which learners meet in class or online, such as news broadcasts or social media posts.
A text, recording or object created for real communication rather than for language teaching, such as a bus timetable, a newspaper report or a product label.
News, interviews, podcasts and other audio or video made for general audiences rather than learners, usually introduced after graded audio and learner podcasts in a listening sequence.
A collection of short real-world texts, such as newspaper extracts, notices and reports, assembled to support the research stage of a project or simulation.
The quality of being genuine in origin or use: a text may be authentic because it was written for real communication, and a task may be authentic because it reflects what learners do outside class.
Comments or corrections on learners’ work generated by software rather than a teacher, such as grammar suggestions in a word processor; it is fast but needs checking for accuracy and relevance.
The use of software to assign scores to spoken or written performances; it raises questions of validity, fairness and transparency, especially when the scores inform important decisions.
Software that analyses learners’ writing and provides scores or feedback on features such as grammar, vocabulary and organization; it is most useful as a supplement to teacher and peer feedback.

Teaching that nurtures learners’ sense of choice and ownership, for example by offering meaningful options, explaining reasons and acknowledging feelings, rather than controlling through pressure (Reeve 2006).
Planning that begins with the intended outcomes, then decides how they will be assessed, and only then chooses activities (Wiggins and McTighe 2005); also called backward planning.
A statement describing the performance expected at one level of a rating scale, such as ‘Band 4: ideas are clearly organized with some linking errors’, used to guide consistent marking.
See Communicational Teaching Project.
Evidence collected before a change is introduced, against which later results can be compared; in action research, a teacher might record pair-talk time in two lessons before trying a new technique.
A reflective cycle in which a teacher states some beliefs about teaching, collects classroom evidence about them, and records any revisions over a term.
The way teachers’ existing beliefs screen new ideas, so that techniques which conflict with those beliefs may be adopted only on the surface (Pajares 1992).
An agreed standard or reference point for judging performance, often illustrated by examples of work at each level, so that different teachers interpret a scale in the same way.
A piece of learner work agreed by raters to illustrate a particular band or level, used in training and calibration to help teachers mark consistently.

The claim that using two languages improves executive functions such as attention control (Bialystok 2001); later studies found inconsistent results (Paap and Greenberg 2013), so the claim is now contested.
A learner-created output, such as a campaign poster, that uses both English and a home language side by side, valuing learners’ languages as a resource.
An automated system whose internal workings cannot be seen or explained, so that users receive a result, such as a score, without reasons for it.
A combination of face-to-face classroom teaching with online or outside-class learning, planned so that each part supports the other (Garrison and Kanuka 2004).
A planning grid showing a unit’s outside-class and in-class activities side by side, so that the teacher can check that every outside task prepares for something in class.
A planned layout of what will be written on the board during a lesson, such as key vocabulary, target structures and the lesson aim, so that the board supports learning clearly.
A programme that supplies classrooms with many high-interest books and time to read them; in Fiji, it produced clear gains in reading (Elley and Mangubhai 1983).
A short, enthusiastic presentation about a book by a teacher or learner, intended to interest others in reading it; regular book talks help build a reading culture in class.
A word or phrase that expresses a writer’s certainty about a claim, such as clearly or demonstrates; with hedges, boosters help writers calibrate claim strength in academic writing.
Understanding a text by building meaning from its smallest parts, such as sounds, letters, words and grammar; it complements top-down processing, which uses background knowledge and expectations.
Giving learners real choices, such as the topic of a project, within limits set by the teacher, such as a theme, time and required outcome.
The number of words a learner knows at least at a basic level of form and meaning; contrast depth of vocabulary knowledge.
A week left free in a scheme of work to absorb lost teaching time, for example from holidays, examinations or events, so the plan stays realistic.

The first stage of the genre-based teaching-learning cycle, in which learners develop knowledge of the topic, for example by researching a local issue in Kannada or Hindi before writing about it in English.
See complexity, accuracy and fluency.
A process in which raters mark the same samples, compare their scores and discuss differences until they apply a rating scale consistently.
A lesson aim written as what learners will be able to do by the end, such as ‘I can ask for and give directions to a place in my town.’
A description of what a learner can do in a language, as in the CEFR, used for setting goals, self-assessment and describing levels; for example, ‘I can write a short email inviting a friend.’
In English for nursing, a written document recording a patient’s needs and planned nursing actions, used as an authentic target genre in designing a specific-purpose course.
See Create a Research Space model.
A method of in-service teacher training in which content passes down from state to district to cluster levels; its risk is that ideas are diluted at each step.
An in-depth study of one person, class or institution in its real context, often using several kinds of data, such as observation, interviews and learners’ work.
See concept-checking question.
See Common European Framework of Reference for Languages.
A planned review point during a project at which the teacher and group check progress and process, give feedback and adjust plans before continuing.
A lesson that brings together and reviews the language and skills taught in preceding lessons, allowing the teacher to check progress before moving on.
Repetition of a word, phrase or sentence by the whole class together after the teacher’s model; useful for pronunciation practice and for building confidence in large classes.
A group of words that is commonly used and stored as a single unit, such as by the way or Could you please…?; learning chunks supports fluency.
A communication strategy in which a speaker who lacks a word describes or explains it instead, such as ‘the thing you use to open a bottle’.
The main position that a speaker or writer argues for; in the simplified claim–reason–evidence structure, it is supported by a reason and an example or evidence (Toulmin 1958).
A move asking a speaker to repeat or explain what they said, such as ‘Sorry, what do you mean?’; it serves both negotiation of meaning and implicit error correction.
The emotional and social atmosphere of a classroom, including how safe learners feel to speak, take risks and make mistakes.
A regular, predictable procedure, such as greeting, taking the register or collecting homework, that saves time and helps learners know what to expect.
See content and language integrated learning.
A unit of work in which a subject topic, such as the water cycle, and the English needed to learn it are planned and taught together, using the 4Cs framework.
Moving between two or more languages within a conversation or sentence; in a multilingual classroom it can be a resource for learning rather than a sign of weakness.
Robinson’s (2001) proposal that more cognitively demanding tasks can increase accuracy and complexity together, rather than forcing a trade-off between them.
The level of thinking a task requires, from recalling and describing to analysing and evaluating; CLIL lessons plan the language needed for each level.
The growth of children’s thinking abilities, such as memory, reasoning and abstraction, over time; it shapes which tasks and explanations suit learners of different ages.
An approach to language that sees it as grounded in general human cognition and experience, and studies meaning through categories, metaphor and constructions.

The amount of mental effort a task places on working memory, which has limited capacity (Sweller 1988); reducing unnecessary load, for example by giving instructions in a home language, frees attention for learning.
The idea that mentally stimulating activities, possibly including lifelong bilingualism, help the brain cope with ageing or damage; evidence for a bilingual effect remains debated.
The quality that makes a text make sense as a whole, with logically connected and relevant ideas; coherence depends on meaning, whereas cohesion depends on visible links.
An analysis identifying why a learner text does not hang together, such as a main point that appears only at the end or a linking word used where no contrast exists.
The linking of sentences and ideas in a text through visible language devices such as pronouns, conjunctions, repetition and synonyms.
A single link between two parts of a text, such as a pronoun referring back to a noun or however connecting two contrasting sentences.
Talk in which learners work together to solve language problems, such as deciding which word fits, which Swain (2000) argued is itself a source of language learning.
The grammatical patterns a word tends to occur with, such as suggest followed by -ing or a that-clause; related to collocation, which concerns word partnerships.
A combination of words that frequently occur together, such as make a decision or heavy rain; learners who know collocations sound more natural and fluent.
The influence that colonial history continues to have on English education, for example in attitudes about the superiority of English or of Western teaching methods.

term: Common European Framework of Reference for Languages
def: An international framework that describes language ability at six levels, from A1 to C2, using can-do descriptors; it is widely used for setting aims and describing levels.
Cummins’s idea that knowledge and skills developed in one language are shared across languages, so literacy developed in a home language supports learning English.

Prabhu’s project in South India (1979–84), in which school classes learned English through problem-solving tasks rather than a grammatical syllabus; one of the earliest large-scale trials of task-based teaching (Prabhu 1987).
The knowledge and ability needed to use language appropriately in real situations, including grammar, social appropriacy, discourse and strategy, not only grammatical correctness (Hymes 1972).
In Chomsky’s (1965) theory, a speaker’s underlying knowledge of language, as distinct from performance, the actual use of language in real situations.
The range and sophistication of the language a learner uses, such as varied vocabulary and subordinate clauses; one of three dimensions of performance, with accuracy and fluency.
A three-part framework for describing learner performance, often abbreviated CAF, used in research and for assessing speaking and writing (Housen and Kuiken 2009).
How easily a listener can understand a speaker, as judged by the listener’s effort; a speaker with a strong accent can still be highly comprehensible.
Language that learners can understand, slightly beyond their current level, which Krashen (1982) argued is the main source of language acquisition.
An approach to teaching listening that places understanding before speaking, giving learners extensive listening before they are asked to produce language.
A question asked to see whether a listener has understood, such as ‘Is that clear?’ or ‘Do you follow?’; used in negotiation of meaning.
A clear idea of what good work looks like, which learners need in order to judge and improve their own work (Sadler 1989); peer assessment helps develop it.
A short question that checks whether learners have understood the meaning of new language, such as ‘Is he still at school?’ after he used to go to school.
A way of understanding one domain of experience in terms of another, reflected in everyday language, such as time as money in spend time or save time (Lakoff and Johnson 1980).
A move in argument that accepts part of an opposing point before responding, such as ‘That is true, but…’; it makes a speaker sound reasonable and persuasive.
A list of all the examples of a word or phrase in a corpus, shown with their context and aligned on the key word, used to study patterns of use.
A short summary of a proposed presentation, submitted to a conference for review, stating the topic, context, methods and main findings or argument.
The tendency to notice and value evidence that supports what we already believe; in action research, a critical friend helps guard against it.
A question that checks whether one has understood a speaker correctly, often by repeating their words, such as ‘You mean Tuesday?’
A factor other than the one being studied that may explain the results; in age research, for example, amount of input may confound the effect of age of arrival.
Natural, fluent speech in which sounds in neighbouring words change, link or disappear, as when want to becomes wanna; learners need practice in hearing it.
The associations and feelings a word carries beyond its basic meaning; for example, slim and skinny both mean thin but differ in connotation.
Activities that help learners notice and work out a grammatical feature for themselves, rather than practising it, often by examining examples and forming a rule.
The aspect of validity concerned with the social consequences of test use, including its effects on teaching and learning (Messick 1989).
A group of two or more consonant sounds together without a vowel between them, as in street or texts; some learners add a vowel to break clusters.
The ability or quality a test aims to measure, such as reading comprehension or speaking fluency; a clear definition of the construct is the basis for valid assessment.
The extent to which a test measures the construct it claims to measure, and not other abilities; for example, whether a writing score reflects writing rather than typing speed.
Language difficulty in a test that is not part of what is being measured, such as complex English in a mathematics test, which can unfairly lower learners’ scores.
In Construction Grammar, a pairing of form and meaning at any size, from single words and chunks to abstract patterns such as She gave him a book.
An approach to grammar that treats language as a network of form–meaning pairings, or constructions, at every level of size and abstraction (Goldberg 1995).
The principle that intended learning outcomes, teaching activities and assessment should all point in the same direction (Biggs and Tang 2011).
An approach in which a subject such as science or geography is taught through an additional language, with planned attention to both content and language.
The choice of which parts of a syllabus a test includes; broad, representative sampling reduces the risk that teaching narrows to match the test.
Language teaching organized around subject matter or themes rather than a language syllabus, so that learners acquire language while learning content.
Features of a teaching context, such as large classes, examinations and limited resources, that may prevent teachers from acting on their beliefs.
A backup plan or activity prepared in case part of a lesson takes more or less time than expected or does not work as planned.

The ongoing learning teachers undertake throughout their careers, through training, reading, reflection, research and collaboration with colleagues, for example in DIET programmes or teacher networks.
A record in which each member of a group notes what they did each week on a project, supporting fair individual assessment and accountability.
Practice in which learners use new language in a limited and supported way, such as drills or gap-fills, with a focus on accuracy.
The main point of a paragraph, usually stated in its topic sentence, which the other sentences in the paragraph develop and support with explanation or examples.
Meaning that a speaker implies rather than states, which the listener infers from context (Grice 1975); for example, ‘It is cold in here’ may be a request to close the window.
Structured group work in which learners depend on one another to achieve a shared goal, while each remains individually accountable.

Grice’s (1975) principle that speakers normally cooperate by making their contributions informative, truthful, relevant and clear; implied meanings often arise when a speaker appears to break one of these maxims.
Roles assigned to group members, such as writer, speaker and checker, that share out participation and responsibility during a task.
A note-taking format with a wide column for notes, a narrow column for cue words or questions, and a summary box at the bottom (Pauk and Owens 2011).
A large, principled collection of real spoken or written texts stored electronically, used to study how language is actually used; plural corpora.
A quick check of a word or phrase in a corpus before teaching it, to confirm how common and natural it is; for example, comparing I have a doubt with I have a question.
A set of symbols used to mark types of error in writing, such as T for tense, so that learners can correct their own mistakes.
A sequence of correction moves, from least to most explicit, that gives learners the chance to self-correct before the teacher supplies the correct form.
A visual plan showing how a course is organized over time, with its strands, units and assessment points; it can be drawn on chart paper or kept as a colour-coded spreadsheet.
A published textbook that provides a structured sequence of material for a language course; teachers can adapt, personalize and supplement it rather than follow it slavishly.
A model of teacher education in which trainees learn by watching and imitating an experienced practitioner (Wallace 1991); contrast the applied science model and the reflective model.
Swales’s (1990) model of how research article introductions establish a territory, identify a gap and occupy the gap; often abbreviated CARS.
A standard licence that lets creators share their work while specifying how others may use, adapt and distribute it, such as with attribution or for non-commercial use only.

Describes assessment that judges performance against fixed criteria or standards, rather than against the performance of other learners; contrast norm-referenced assessment, which ranks learners against one another.
An approach to applied linguistics that examines questions of power, inequality and ideology in language use and language education (Pennycook 2001).
A brief review of a unit or material through a critical lens, asking whose voices, views and values are included or left out.
The ability to evaluate critically the practices and values of one’s own and other cultures, a key element of intercultural communicative competence (Byram 1997).
An approach to studying how language use reflects, reproduces or challenges relations of power, for example by asking who is presented as acting and who as acted upon (Fairclough 1989).
A trusted colleague who asks challenging questions and offers honest feedback on a teacher’s work or research, including other possible explanations for results.
An event, often small, that prompts reflection and learning; in intercultural learning, a brief case of misunderstanding between people from different cultures.
Awareness of how language is used to shape views and maintain power, which language education should help learners develop (Fairclough 1992).
An approach to education that aims to help learners question social injustice and act to change it, associated with Paulo Freire (1970).
The hypothesis that there is a limited period in life during which a language can be acquired to native-like levels (Lenneberg 1967); its application to second languages is debated.
Reflection that goes beyond what worked to question the assumptions, values and wider social and institutional conditions behind teaching practice, and whose interests it serves.
The development in applied linguistics and ELT of attention to power, identity and inequality, which situates established techniques in their social context rather than replacing them.
A learner who shares knowledge of their own culture, customs or community with the class, treating learners’ experiences as a resource for intercultural learning.
An approach to teaching literature that treats texts as a means of understanding the culture, history and values from which they come (Carter and Long 1991).
A final task at the end of a unit that draws on all the language and skills taught, such as a group presentation or campaign.
The overall plan for education in a subject or institution, including its aims, content, methods and assessment; in India, national frameworks such as NCF 2023 guide state curricula.
The tendency for teaching to focus only on what is tested, leaving out other valuable content and skills, such as speaking, when an examination tests only reading and writing.

The score on a test that divides one level or decision from another, such as pass and fail; setting it requires careful judgement because small differences in score can lead to very different decisions.
An approach in which learners examine concordance lines from a corpus and work out patterns for themselves, acting as researchers (Johns 1991).
The final stage of a role-play or simulation, in which learners discuss how it went and the teacher gives feedback on language and task performance.
The quality of words that look as if their meaning can be worked out from their parts but cannot, such as outline (not ‘out’ + ‘line’) (Laufer 1989).
(1) In reading, turning written symbols into sounds and words. (2) In listening, turning the sound stream into words, as distinct from meaning building (Field 2008).
Kumaravadivelu’s (2016) call for teachers outside the traditional centres of ELT to stop waiting for methods from the West and develop their own.
Examining and challenging the colonial roots of English language teaching, such as assumptions about native-speaker authority and Western methods, and valuing local knowledge and practices.
In the genre-based teaching-learning cycle, the stage in which the teacher and learners analyse a model text to understand its purpose, structure and language; also called modelling.
Teaching that presents a rule first and then asks learners to apply it in examples; contrast inductive teaching, in which learners work out the rule.
Describing learners in terms of what they lack rather than what they can do or need; for example, ‘weak learners’ rather than ‘learners who need more time’.
Correcting errors after an activity has finished rather than during it, so that learners can focus on fluency and communication.
A test given some time after an intervention to check whether learning has lasted, not just appeared immediately afterwards; it is important when evaluating claims made for new methods or technology.
How well a learner knows a word, including its forms, meanings, collocations, register and use in context; contrast breadth of vocabulary knowledge.
The planning decision of how far to cover many topics briefly or fewer topics in greater depth, often by marking syllabus items as essential, important or optional.
A record of the decisions a teacher makes in writing a material, such as the choice of text and task, linked to principles and revised in the light of classroom evidence.
A written plan in which a teacher sets professional development goals for a period, with concrete actions, the support needed and dates for reviewing progress.
An error that reflects a natural stage in learning a language, such as goed for went, rather than interference from the first language.
A person who argues against a position, not necessarily from belief, to test the strength of an argument and encourage deeper thinking; in class, the role can be assigned in discussions.
An approach in which a teacher treats learners’ errors and difficulties as evidence to be analysed in order to decide what to teach next.
A test designed to identify learners’ specific strengths and weaknesses in order to plan teaching; contrast a placement test, which assigns learners to a level.
Speech in which two or more people interact and build meaning together, as in conversation; contrast monologic speech, as in a presentation.
A situation in which a test item behaves differently for groups of equal ability, such as learners from different language backgrounds, suggesting possible bias.
Adapting teaching, tasks, support or outcomes so that learners of different levels and needs in the same class can all make progress.
The gap between those who have access to digital devices, the internet and the skills to use them and those who do not.
Software, applications and online platforms, such as Google Forms or Padlet, used to support teaching, learning and assessment, both in class and outside it.

Corrective feedback in which the teacher supplies the correct form, for example by crossing out goed and writing went above it. It is quick and clear, and useful when learners cannot yet correct the error themselves.

Ways of working with teachers in mentoring and supervision: a directive mentor tells the teacher what to change, while a non-directive mentor listens and asks questions so the teacher reaches their own decisions (Freeman 1982).

A written medical document given when a patient leaves hospital, setting out diagnosis, treatment and instructions. In a nursing English course it is a target genre, for example read in English and explained to the patient in Kannada.

The study of language beyond the sentence: how texts and conversations are organized, how they hang together and how meaning depends on context. It helps teachers explain features such as cohesion, turn-taking and information order.
A group that shares goals, genres and specialized language, such as nurses, engineers or academic researchers, and recognizes what counts as a good text in its field (Swales 1990).

The ability to combine sentences and utterances into coherent, cohesive spoken or written texts, for example by linking ideas and signalling the organization of a talk. It was added to the model of communicative competence by Canale (1983).
A word or phrase that organizes talk or writing and signals how ideas relate, such as so, anyway, well, however or on the other hand. Spoken markers are often missing from coursebook dialogues.

In item analysis, a measure of how well a test item separates stronger from weaker learners, calculated simply as the facility value in the top-scoring group minus the facility value in the bottom-scoring group.

A question to which the teacher already knows the answer, asked to check knowledge or display language, such as ‘What’s the capital of Karnataka?’ It contrasts with a genuine question (Long and Sato 1983).

An approach to teaching that minimizes published materials and technology and builds lessons from the conversation and language that learners bring to class (Meddings and Thornbury 2009). It is also known as ‘teaching unplugged’.

The part of a language portfolio in which learners keep selected samples of their work, such as drafts, finished pieces and recordings, as evidence of what they can do in the language (Council of Europe 2001).

Having two markers, human or human and machine, score the same piece of work independently, so that disagreements can be checked. It is used to monitor reliability and to keep human oversight of automated scoring.

In a rights-based framework, the person or institution responsible for making a right real, such as the state or a school under the Right to Education Act, as distinct from the right-holder, the child.

Assessment that combines testing with mediation: the assessor offers graduated help during the task and notes how much the learner needs, revealing what they can do with support as well as alone (Poehner 2008).

A specific learning difficulty that mainly affects accurate and fluent word reading and spelling, despite adequate teaching and ability. Learners benefit from multisensory phonics, extra time and teaching that does not depend on reading instructions alone.

The teacher habit of repeating each learner’s answer to the class, as in ‘Bengaluru, yes, Bengaluru is the capital.’ It increases teacher talk and teaches learners to listen to the teacher rather than to each other.
The final stage of process writing, in which learners check and correct grammar, spelling and punctuation after the content and organization have been revised, often using a short editing checklist.

The digital and non-digital tools used to support teaching and learning, from projectors and apps to learning platforms such as DIKSHA. Its value depends on purpose and pedagogy rather than on the tool itself.

A statistic showing how large a difference or relationship is, in a standard unit, rather than only whether it is statistically significant. Meta-analyses combine effect sizes from many studies into an average.

Drawing language, ideas or answers out of learners through questions, prompts, pictures or gestures instead of simply telling them. As corrective feedback, it prompts learners to self-correct, for example ‘Yesterday I…?’
The loss of a sound in connected speech, as when next day is pronounced /neks deɪ/ or mustn’t loses its /t/. Recognizing elision helps learners understand natural, fast speech.
The omission of words that can be understood from context, as in ‘You free?’ for ‘Are you free?’ It is common in conversation and a key feature of spoken grammar.

A learner who is just beginning to read, linking sounds to letters and recognizing some familiar words. Teachers plan oral-first activities and introduce written English gradually, building on home-language literacy.
The tendency for emotions to spread from one person to others in a group. In class, a teacher’s enthusiasm or anxiety can quickly shape the mood and willingness to speak of the whole room.

Learners’ active involvement in a task, cognitively, emotionally and socially. With digital activities, a useful check is how much English learners actually produced, heard or read, and whether they interacted with each other.

English used as a shared language between speakers who have different first languages, such as an Indian and a Japanese engineer. Research focuses on mutual intelligibility rather than conformity to native-speaker norms (Seidlhofer 2011).

Teaching English for study in further and higher education, focusing on academic genres, reading, listening to lectures, citation and argument. It developed out of the wider English for Specific Purposes movement.

Teaching English for a particular professional or academic need, such as nursing, engineering or hospitality, with content and tasks drawn from analysis of the learners’ target situations (Hutchinson and Waters 1987).

The positive emotion learners feel when a class is both challenging and satisfying. Research on foreign language enjoyment suggests it matters as much as anxiety and supports learning (Dewaele and MacIntyre 2014).

A systematic deviation from the target language that reflects a learner’s current knowledge, as distinct from a mistake, a slip the learner can correct. Errors show the learner’s developing system and are a natural part of learning.
The systematic study of learners’ errors, identifying, classifying and explaining them to understand the learner’s developing system and plan teaching (Corder 1967).
A record kept by the learner of their own errors, usually in three columns: what I wrote or said, the correct version, and my rule or reminder. It supports self-monitoring and learner autonomy.
A Council of Europe document in which learners record and reflect on their language learning, with three parts: a language passport, a language biography and a dossier (Council of Europe 2001).
In a spoken or written argument, the facts, examples or data that support a reason and a claim. Learners practise the simple structure claim, reason, example or evidence.

Matching the confidence of a claim to the strength of the research behind it, for example ‘several large studies agree’ versus ‘one small study suggests’. Teacher educators model it when they cite research.
Teaching in which decisions are grounded in systematic research findings about what works. Critics note that classroom contexts vary, so research should inform rather than dictate practice.

Teaching in which research evidence is one input, weighed alongside professional judgement, learners’ needs and local context. The term is often preferred to ‘evidence-based’ because it gives teachers a stronger role.

A transferable technique for doing well in a test, such as skimming questions before reading, managing time across sections or eliminating wrong options. It should support, not replace, development of the abilities the exam measures.
A document specifying the content, question types, marks and weighting of an examination, such as a board examination blueprint. Teachers use it to align term plans with assessment requirements.

A set of cognitive processes that control attention and behaviour, including inhibitory control, switching between tasks and working memory. Claims that bilingualism improves executive function are now debated (Bialystok 2001; Paap and Greenberg 2013).
A short task learners complete at the end of a lesson, such as one sentence using the target language or an answer to a question. It gives the teacher quick evidence for planning the next lesson.
In Kachru’s model of World Englishes, countries where English has no historical or official role but is widely learned as a foreign language, such as China, Japan and Brazil (Kachru 1985).
Helping learners form realistic beliefs about how fast they will progress, for example preparing them for the slower gains of the intermediate plateau so that they do not lose motivation.
In a jigsaw activity, a group of learners who study the same text or topic together before returning to their home groups to teach it to others.
A teacher who combines secure classroom skills with specialist depth and a principled understanding of theory and research, and who can explain and adapt their decisions to context.
A self-assessment in which a teacher rates their own knowledge and skills across several areas, supported by evidence and a colleague’s view, to set priorities for professional development.

Three separate ways of relating to a language: how well a person uses it, how far they identify with it, and whether they were born into it (Rampton 1990). The distinction challenges the idea of the ‘native speaker’.

The degree to which an automated system, such as an AI scoring tool, can give understandable reasons for its decisions. Many systems work as a ‘black box’, which raises fairness concerns in high-stakes assessment.
Learning in which the learner is aware of what is being learned, often with conscious attention to rules or forms, such as studying a grammar rule or a word list. It contrasts with implicit learning.

A form of teacher research that begins with an exploration stage, gathering evidence to understand a classroom issue, before planning any change (Smith and Rebolledo 2018). It has been used in teacher-research schemes in India.

A form of practitioner research in which teachers and learners work together to understand puzzles in their classroom life, using normal teaching activities as the means of investigation (Allwright and Hanks 2009).
Talk in which learners engage critically but constructively with each other’s ideas, giving reasons, asking questions and thinking aloud together (Barnes 1976; Mercer 2000).
An additional, more challenging task for learners who finish early or need stretch, designed to deepen the same learning rather than simply add more of the same work.

Listening to large amounts of easy, enjoyable material, such as graded audio, podcasts or radio, for general meaning and pleasure. It builds listening fluency and complements shorter, intensive listening lessons.

Reading large quantities of easy, self-selected material for pleasure and general understanding, such as graded readers or StoryWeaver books (Day and Bamford 1998). It builds fluency, vocabulary and reading habits.
A reward that comes from outside the activity, such as points, badges or prizes. In gamified learning it can raise short-term participation but may weaken interest in the activity itself.

A person’s public self-image. Positive face is the wish to be liked and approved of; negative face is the wish not to be imposed upon. Requests, criticisms and disagreement threaten face (Brown and Levinson 1987).
In item analysis, the proportion of test-takers who answer an item correctly, from 0 to 1. A value of 0.93 means almost everyone got it right, so the item tells the teacher little.
A cycle in which feedback leads to action and the result is checked, for example comment, revision and review. Without closing the loop, feedback on homework or writing has little effect.
Reviewing the quality of the feedback learners give each other, using a checklist of qualities such as specific, linked to criteria and kind, so that peer feedback improves over time.
A sound or word used to hold a turn or gain planning time in speech, such as um, er or well. Fillers are normal in natural conversation but usually absent from coursebook dialogues.
The gradual loss of proficiency in a first language, usually when a speaker has little opportunity to use it, for example after moving early to a place where another language dominates.

An external obstacle to using technology in teaching, such as lack of devices, connectivity or time. It contrasts with second-order barriers, which are teachers’ beliefs and confidence (Ertmer and Ottenbreit-Leftwich 2010).
Grouping learners in different ways for different purposes, by level, interest or mixed ability, and changing groups regularly so that no learner is fixed in one ‘level’.
A model in which learners meet new input outside class, for example through a short video or reading, so that class time can be used for interaction and practice (Bergmann and Sams 2012).
The ability to speak or write at a natural speed with limited hesitation, focusing on meaning. It is often balanced against accuracy and complexity in planning tasks and giving feedback.
A small group of learners, perhaps five to eight, whom the teacher monitors closely in a given lesson, rotating so that every learner is observed regularly, even in a class of fifty.
Briefly drawing learners’ attention to language forms as they arise during meaning-focused activity, such as a task or discussion (Long 1991). It contrasts with focus on forms.
Teaching language forms as the main content of lessons, one by one, often through presentation and practice of a pre-selected grammar point (Long 1991). It contrasts with focus on form.
Corrective feedback that targets one or a few selected error types, such as past tense forms, rather than every error in a piece of work. It is usually easier for learners to act on.

In stylistics, making a feature of a text stand out through repetition, parallelism or deviation from normal usage, such as unusual word order or a sudden change of tense (Short 1996). Learners discuss what effect it creates.
The worry and nervousness specific to using or learning a foreign language, such as fear of speaking in front of others or of negative evaluation (Horwitz, Horwitz and Cope 1986).
The pattern by which memory of newly learned material drops quickly and then more slowly over time unless it is reviewed (Ebbinghaus 1885). It is the basis for spaced review of vocabulary.
Making learners familiar with an exam’s format, question types and timing so that unfamiliarity does not lower their scores. It should take a smaller share of course time than skill development.
Assessment used during learning to guide the next steps in teaching and learning, through questioning, observation, feedback and self- and peer assessment (Black and Wiliam 1998).
A planned point in a unit of work where the teacher checks learners’ progress, for example with a short task, and adjusts the rest of the unit in response.
The persistence of certain errors in a learner’s language despite further exposure and teaching, such as a stable He go in an otherwise advanced speaker (Selinker 1972).
The basic ability to read with understanding and write, expected by the end of Grade 3. NEP 2020 and the NIPUN Bharat mission give it high priority in India’s early grades.
A group member who contributes little and benefits from others’ work. Cooperative learning reduces free riding through individual accountability and clear roles.
A lesson stage in which learners use the target language with less teacher control and more choice, for example in a discussion or role-play, following controlled practice.
How often a word, phrase or structure occurs in a corpus of real language. It helps teachers decide which items to teach first and how much time to give them.
A group of words ranked by frequency, such as the most common 1,000 or 2,000 words. Knowing a learner’s frequency band helps teachers choose readable texts and target vocabulary.

The view that adult second language learners still have access to Universal Grammar, so that their grammars are constrained by it even when first-language features transfer at the start (Schwartz and Sprouse 1996).
The purpose a piece of language serves in communication, such as requesting, apologizing, advising or agreeing. A functional syllabus organizes teaching around such purposes (Wilkins 1976).
A syllabus organized around language functions, such as requesting or suggesting, and notions, such as time, quantity or location, rather than grammatical structures (Wilkins 1976).

The proposal that adult second language learning differs fundamentally from child first language acquisition, relying on first-language knowledge and general problem-solving rather than Universal Grammar (Bley-Vroman 1989).
Adding game elements such as points, levels, badges and leaderboards to learning activities to increase motivation. Its benefits depend on whether the language work itself remains central.

Controlling access to education, jobs or migration through requirements such as English proficiency or high-stakes test scores. In India, English often acts as a gatekeeper to higher education and employment.

Artificial intelligence that produces new text, images or audio in response to prompts, such as chatbots based on large language models. It offers teaching possibilities but can produce confident errors.
A type of text with a recognized social purpose and typical stages and language, such as a recount, a complaint letter, a lab report or a nursing handover.
Analysing examples of a genre to identify its purpose, typical moves or stages and characteristic language, so that learners can be taught to produce it (Swales 1990).
A ranked list of the genres learners need in their target situation, based on needs analysis, such as a nursing course listing care plans, handovers and lectures in order of importance.
The genre that a task’s outcome should take, such as a one-minute spoken recommendation. Setting it changes what counts as a successful task and focuses the report and language-focus stages.
An assessment rubric whose criteria reflect the purpose, stages and language of a particular genre, rather than generic features that apply to any text.

An approach to teaching writing, and speaking, that makes the stages and language of genres explicit through a teaching-learning cycle of building the field, deconstruction, joint construction and independent construction. It is associated with the Sydney School.
A question to which the asker does not already know the answer, such as ‘What do you think?’ It invites real communication, unlike a display question.
A property of a text produced for a real audience and purpose, not for learners. Widdowson (1978) distinguished it from authenticity, which depends on how a reader engages with the text.
The general meaning or main idea of a text. Reading or listening for gist means getting an overall understanding without attending to every detail, often as a first task.
The tendency for English sentences to begin with information already known to the reader (given) and end with new information (Halliday 1985). Applying it helps learners write prose that flows.

A broad term for countries of Africa, Asia, Latin America and the Pacific, often formerly colonized. In ELT it draws attention to scholarship and practice from these regions, including India, that are under-represented.
Helping learners set specific, achievable learning goals, such as ‘use five new phrases in a conversation this week’, and review them. It is a core step in developing learner autonomy.
Listening material, such as audiobooks of graded readers, written and recorded within a controlled vocabulary and grammar level, so that learners can listen extensively with ease.
A book written or adapted for language learners within a controlled range of vocabulary and grammar, used for extensive reading at the right level.
Adjusting the difficulty of materials or tasks for a group of learners, by changing the language demand, the task demand, or both, often one at a time so the cause of difficulty is clear.

Adjusting the difficulty of what learners must do with a text rather than simplifying the text itself. With an authentic notice, for example, weaker learners find three facts while stronger learners interpret its tone.

A sequence in which responsibility moves step by step from teacher to learner: the teacher models, then learners work with support, then independently (Pearson and Gallagher 1983). It is often summarized as ‘I do, we do, you do’.
One of a sequence of hints that move from implicit to explicit, given only as far as a learner needs to self-correct (Aljaafreh and Lantolf 1994). It is used in dynamic assessment.
Knowledge of the vocabulary, grammar, pronunciation and spelling of a language, one component of communicative competence (Canale and Swain 1980).

Expressing a meaning in a less direct grammatical form, especially turning processes into nouns, as in analyse becoming analysis (Halliday and Martin 1993). It makes academic writing dense and abstract.
A visual framework, such as a table, flowchart, Venn diagram or mind map, that helps learners organize ideas or information from a text before speaking or writing.
In cooperative learning, time for groups to reflect on how well they worked together and what to improve, for example at the end of a task.
Specific responsibilities assigned to members of a group, such as leader, note-taker, timekeeper or reporter, to structure participation and reduce free riding.
The belief that ability can grow through effort, good strategies and help, as opposed to a fixed mindset, which sees ability as unchangeable (Dweck 2006).
Working out the meaning of an unknown word from clues in the surrounding text, such as examples, contrasts or word parts. It is a key strategy for extensive reading.
A way of teaching in which learners work out a rule or pattern from examples, guided by the teacher’s questions, rather than being told the rule first.
In nursing, the spoken and written transfer of patient information between shifts. In an English for Specific Purposes course for nurses, it is a high-priority spoken target genre.
In Universal Grammar, the setting that decides whether heads such as verbs come before or after their complements. English is head-initial (read books); Kannada and Hindi are head-final.
Using language to soften a claim or show caution, such as may, seems, perhaps or it could be argued. It is important in academic writing and in polite disagreement.

A person who grew up with a home language that is not the main language of their wider community, such as a Kannada-speaking child raised in Mumbai. Heritage speakers often understand more than they can say (Montrul 2008; Polinsky 2018).
Grouping learners of different abilities, backgrounds or languages together so that they can support and learn from each other, as in many cooperative learning structures.
An assessment whose results have major consequences for the test-taker, such as admission, certification, employment or migration. Board examinations and international English tests are examples.
A report card recommended by NEP 2020 that describes a learner’s development across many areas, including self- and peer assessment, rather than reporting marks alone.
Assessing a performance as a whole and giving a single overall score or band, rather than separate scores for criteria such as content, organization and accuracy.
Work learners do outside class. Well-designed homework extends class work, fits learners’ real circumstances, uses spaced practice and teaches independent study habits.
A set of homework options at different levels of independence, such as a structured exercise, a guided writing task and an open project, from which learners choose.
Keeping trained people responsible for checking and, where necessary, overriding automated decisions, such as AI-generated scores, especially in high-stakes assessment.
An approach to AI in education that keeps human agency, wellbeing and teacher judgement at the centre, with attention to data protection and age-appropriate use (UNESCO 2023).
Krashen’s formula for comprehensible input: language slightly beyond the learner’s current level (i), made understandable by context, which he argued drives acquisition (Krashen 1985).
Reading material just below the learner’s current level, so that attention can go to meaning and enjoyment. It is the recommended level for extensive reading (Day and Bamford 1998).
See instruction-checking question.
The image of the person a learner would like to become as a user of the second language, such as a confident English-speaking engineer. It is a key source of motivation (Dörnyei 2009).
A piece of work, written, spoken or multimodal, in which learners invest their identities and which reflects them back positively, often using home languages (Cummins and Early 2011).

A set of beliefs that come to seem natural and common sense within a society, such as the belief that only one ‘standard’ English is correct. Critical approaches ask whose interests such beliefs serve.

A basic mental pattern formed through bodily experience, such as CONTAINER, PATH or UP–DOWN, that underlies the meaning of many words, for example the particles in in, out, up and down (Johnson 1987).
Meaning that a listener infers beyond what is literally said, based on shared assumptions about cooperative communication (Grice 1975). ‘It’s cold in here’ may imply ‘Please close the window.’
Professional development for practising teachers, such as DIET workshops, school-based mentoring or online courses, as distinct from pre-service teacher education before entering the profession.
Learning that happens without deliberate intention, as a by-product of doing something else, such as picking up words while reading a story for pleasure.
The situation in which a heritage speaker’s home language is not fully developed because exposure decreased in childhood, often once schooling began in another language (Montrul 2008).
The stage of a genre teaching-learning cycle in which learners write a text of the genre on their own, after deconstruction and joint construction, using genre-referenced criteria.
The variety of English used in India, with its own features of pronunciation, vocabulary and grammar, such as prepone or co-brother. It is a legitimate variety of English in its own right.
Corrective feedback that shows an error has been made, for example by underlining or using a code, without supplying the correct form, so that learners correct it themselves.
An utterance whose intended function differs from its grammatical form, such as ‘Can you open the window?’, which is a request rather than a question about ability (Searle 1975).
In cooperative learning, the principle that each member is responsible for their own learning and contribution, checked for example by an individual quiz after group work.
A written plan for a learner with special educational needs, setting specific goals, support strategies and review dates, agreed with parents and specialists.
Teaching in which learners meet examples first and work out the rule or pattern themselves, as opposed to deductive teaching, which begins with the rule.
Working out meaning that is not directly stated in a text, using clues and background knowledge, such as a character’s feelings or a writer’s attitude.
An activity in which learners hold different information and must communicate to complete a task, such as finding differences between two pictures or completing a timetable.
The ability to suppress an automatic or irrelevant response, such as naming the ink colour of the word red printed in blue. It is one component of executive function.
In Kachru’s model of World Englishes, countries where English is the primary language of most people, such as the UK, the USA and Australia (Kachru 1985).
Silent, internal speech used for thinking and planning. In sociocultural theory, it develops from social speech via private speech as learners internalize language.
A short question that checks learners have understood what to do, such as ‘Are you writing or speaking?’ or ‘How many minutes do you have?’, rather than ‘Do you understand?’
Motivation to learn a language for practical benefits, such as passing an examination or getting a job (Gardner and Lambert 1972).
A citation in which the author’s name is part of the sentence, as in ‘Rao (2022) argues…’, as opposed to non-integral citation, where the name appears only in brackets (Swales 1990).
An extended project, over several weeks, that combines skills and stages such as research, simulation, debate and presentation to produce a real outcome for a real audience.
Teaching listening, speaking, reading and writing together, as they are used in real life, rather than as separate subjects, for example reading an article and then discussing and writing about it.
A lesson in which several skills work together towards one outcome, often built on a task cycle with a genre target and cooperative roles.
Motivation to learn a language because of interest in, or a wish to connect with, its speakers and their culture (Gardner and Lambert 1972).
The extent to which a speaker’s words can be understood by listeners. Many teachers now aim for international intelligibility rather than a native-speaker accent (Jenkins 2000).
Close, focused listening to a short passage for specific detail or language features, usually with tasks and replays, as distinct from extensive listening.
Close, detailed reading of a short text, often with attention to vocabulary, grammar and meaning, as distinct from extensive reading for pleasure.
A short document attached to a test specification that explains what each section is meant to encourage in the classroom, with examples of good and poor preparation, to promote positive washback.
The degree to which different markers give the same score to the same performance. It is improved by clear rubrics, benchmark samples and standardization meetings.
The proposal that conversational interaction, especially negotiation of meaning, promotes acquisition by making input comprehensible and drawing attention to form (Long 1996).
The way learners are organized to interact in a stage of a lesson, such as teacher–class, pairs, groups or individual work.
The proportion of class time learners spend interacting in English. It is one measure of whether a change such as flipping the classroom has freed time for practice.
A change speakers make to conversation to overcome communication problems, such as a clarification request, confirmation check or repetition. It is central to negotiation of meaning.
The ability to communicate effectively and appropriately with people from other cultures, combining language skills with attitudes, knowledge and skills of interpreting and relating (Byram 1997).
The study of how writing conventions differ across cultures and how writers negotiate them, without assuming that one culture’s patterns are superior (Connor 2011).
Mutual reliance between learners, or between learners and teachers. Autonomy grows through interdependence and dialogue rather than isolation (Little 1991).
The passing of a language from parents to children in the home. Its breakdown is the most important sign that a language is endangered.
A planned point during a project where learners produce a small, visible output, so that the teacher can check progress and give feedback before the final product.
The developing language system of a second language learner, which has its own rules and differs from both the first language and the target language (Selinker 1972).
A stage at which learners, usually at intermediate level, feel they are no longer making progress despite continued study (Richards 2008).
In sociocultural theory, the process by which knowledge and skills first shared in social interaction become part of an individual’s independent thinking and ability.
The set of reasonable interpretations a literary text allows. Assessment criteria for literary response should reward well-supported readings within this range rather than one ‘correct’ answer.
In action research, the planned change a teacher makes in order to address a classroom question, described clearly enough that its effects can be observed and evaluated.
The rise and fall of pitch in speech, which signals meaning, attitude and information structure, such as the difference between a question and a statement.
An error caused by the target language itself, such as overgeneralizing a rule (goed, childs), rather than by first-language influence (Richards 1971).
Learners’ commitment to learning a language, understood in relation to their identity and the social and economic value they expect the language to bring (Norton 2013).
Analysing how each test item performed, using statistics such as facility value and discrimination index, to identify items that are too easy, too hard or faulty.
A cooperative structure in which each group member studies a different part of the material in an expert group, then teaches it to their home group, so that all parts are needed to complete the task.
A stage of a genre teaching-learning cycle in which teacher and class write a text together, with the teacher thinking aloud about the writer’s decisions.
Planning in which a subject teacher and an English teacher work together to set content outcomes, language demands and support, as in content and language integrated learning.

A model of World Englishes with three concentric circles: the Inner Circle, where English is a native language; the Outer Circle, including India, where it is a second language; and the Expanding Circle (Kachru 1985).

The unequal relationship in which ELT theory, methods and materials flow mainly from Anglophone ‘centre’ countries to the ‘periphery’, whose own knowledge and practice are under-recognized (Phillipson 1992).
The influence of a learner’s first language on their use or learning of another language. It can help, as with shared vocabulary, or cause errors, as with word order.
People’s beliefs and feelings about languages, varieties and accents, such as prestige attached to certain accents, which affect how speakers are judged and how learners feel.
The decline in proficiency in a language a person once knew, caused by reduced use. It can affect both first and second languages.
The part of a language portfolio in which learners describe their language learning experiences, set goals and reflect on their progress (Council of Europe 2001).
Recording and archiving a language, including audio and video of speakers, texts, dictionaries and grammars, especially for endangered languages, so that they can be studied, taught and revitalized.
The situation in which a language is at risk of no longer being spoken, usually because children are no longer learning it (Krauss 1992).
A stage in a lesson, especially at the end of a task cycle, where learners examine and practise language features that arose during the task (Willis 1996).
In the CLIL Language Triptych, the language learners need to take part in learning, such as asking questions, working in groups and presenting (Coyle, Hood and Marsh 2010).
Keeping a language alive and in use, whether a community keeping its language despite pressure to shift, or an individual keeping proficiency after formal study ends.

In literature teaching, the model that uses literary texts to develop learners’ language knowledge and awareness (Carter and Long 1991). It is one of three models, with the cultural and personal growth models.
An early childhood programme in which young children are cared for entirely in an endangered language, as in the Māori Kōhanga Reo in New Zealand (Hinton and Hale 2001).
In the CLIL Language Triptych, the subject-specific language needed to understand and express content, such as the terms for photosynthesis (Coyle, Hood and Marsh 2010).
The part of a language portfolio that summarizes a learner’s languages, self-assessed levels, certificates and intercultural experiences (Council of Europe 2001).
An activity in which learners colour a body outline to show their languages and how they relate to them. It reveals the richness of learners’ linguistic repertoires (Busch 2012).
The process by which a community gradually replaces one language with another in more and more domains, often over generations.
In the CLIL Language Triptych, the new language that emerges as learners think, discuss and learn content (Coyle, Hood and Marsh 2010).
The strength of a language in terms of its use and transmission, assessed by factors such as whether children still learn it at home (UNESCO Ad Hoc Expert Group on Endangered Languages 2003).

An approach to materials design that starts from a pre-selected grammar or vocabulary item and builds texts and activities to present it, in contrast to a text-driven approach, which starts from an engaging text and draws language work from it.

Using language, spoken or written, to make sense of a problem and shape one’s thinking about it (Swain 2006); for example, pairs talking through why a sentence needs has rather than have while correcting it.

A class whose size makes individual attention, movement and marking difficult; in many Indian government schools this means forty to sixty or more learners on fixed benches, calling for routines such as pair work, row leaders and peer checking.

A generative AI system trained on vast amounts of text to predict and produce fluent language in response to prompts, such as ChatGPT; useful for practice and materials, but it can produce confident errors that teachers must check.

The visual arrangement of text, headings, images, white space and instructions on a page or screen; clear, consistent layout makes materials easier to follow, especially when worksheets are photocopied in black and white.

The short opening stage of a lesson that engages learners’ interest, activates what they already know about the topic and prepares them for the main input; for example, showing a photo of a local market before a shopping dialogue.

The capacity to take charge of one’s own learning, including setting goals, choosing materials and methods, and evaluating progress (Holec 1981); it is developed gradually, through guided choices, rather than simply handed over.

A principled electronic collection of texts produced by learners of a language, used to identify common errors and patterns at a given level; a teacher can compile one from a cohort’s essays for error analysis.
Learners’ sense that a task or project genuinely belongs to them, fostered by giving real choices over topic, roles or outcome within agreed limits; ownership tends to increase effort and commitment.

What learners say they want from teaching, for example a particular accent model or type of teacher; preferences are worth researching and discussing, but they are often shaped by assumptions rather than by learners’ real communicative needs.
A simple record of an individual learner’s background, languages, interests, level and needs, built up at the start of a course and updated over time to guide planning and support.

A written agreement, negotiated between learner and teacher, that sets out the learner’s goals, the activities and resources to be used, a timeline and how progress will be evaluated; a brief ‘mini’ version can be built into a single unit.

A regular written or recorded reflection in which learners note what they have learnt, what they found difficult and what they plan to do next; it supports reflection and autonomy, and may be written partly in the home language.

The specific actions and techniques learners use to make learning easier and more effective, such as guessing meaning from context, grouping vocabulary or planning before speaking (Oxford 1990); many can be taught explicitly.

Learners’ supposed preferred ways of taking in information, such as visual or auditory; research has not shown that matching teaching to a learner’s style improves learning, so varied, multimodal teaching is the safer choice.

In course design, especially ESP, the analysis of the conditions in which a course will run, such as time available, class size, resources, and teachers’ and learners’ expectations, alongside analysis of target needs.

A spaced-repetition method, devised by Sebastian Leitner, in which flashcards move between boxes: a card answered correctly moves to a box reviewed less often, and a card answered wrongly goes back to the first box.
A clear statement of what learners should be able to do by the end of a lesson, ideally written as a can-do statement, for example ‘Learners can ask for and give directions to places in their town’.
A brief record kept by the teacher of what happened in a lesson, including good examples and problems noticed while monitoring, used to plan feedback and later lessons.
One distinct phase of a lesson with its own purpose, such as lead-in, presentation, controlled practice, freer practice or wrap-up; each stage should prepare learners for the next.

A collaborative form of professional development, originating in Japan, in which teachers jointly plan a lesson, one teaches it while colleagues observe learners, and the group then discusses and revises the lesson.
A sequence of related words running through a text, such as repetitions, synonyms or words from the same field (rain, monsoon, flood), which helps to hold the text together and signal its topic.
A multi-word unit stored and used as a whole, such as by the way or I’d like to; the lexical approach treats such chunks as central to fluency (Lewis 1993).
The way a text is held together through vocabulary choices, such as repetition, synonyms, superordinates and collocation, rather than through grammatical links (Halliday and Hasan 1976).

The theory that each word becomes associated, through repeated encounters, with the words, grammar and contexts it typically occurs with, so that speakers expect and reproduce these patterns (Hoey 2005).
A syllabus organized around the most frequent words, their meanings and the patterns they occur in, typically based on corpus evidence (Willis 1990).

Continuing, self-directed learning across one’s life and career, beyond formal education; for teachers, it includes reading, reflection, peer learning and classroom inquiry long after initial training.

The idea that learners can attend to only so much at once, so that focusing on fluency, accuracy or complexity may come at the expense of the others (Skehan 1998); planning time and task repetition can ease this pressure.

A set of pronunciation features, identified by Jennifer Jenkins (2000), that appear most important for intelligibility when English is used between non-native speakers, such as most consonant sounds and nuclear stress.
Ideologies and practices that legitimize and reproduce unequal power and resources between groups defined by language (Skutnabb-Kangas 1988); a form of linguistic discrimination.

Unfair treatment of people on the basis of their language, dialect or accent, for example rejecting a qualified teacher because of a regional Indian accent rather than for any problem with intelligibility.

The relationships between languages and their speakers within a society and its environment (Haugen 1972); the term draws attention to how one language’s growth, such as English, can affect the health of others.

The rights of individuals and communities to use, learn and be educated in their own languages, including the right to learn an official language; the idea is closely associated with Tove Skutnabb-Kangas and Robert Phillipson.
The dominance of one language, especially English, maintained through unequal structural and cultural relations that favour it over other languages (Phillipson 1992).

A group whose language differs from the dominant or official language of the region or state; India’s Constitution provides for instruction in the mother tongue for linguistic minority children at the primary stage.
The whole set of languages, dialects, registers and styles that a person can draw on; a learner in Bengaluru may use Kannada, Tamil, Hindi and English for different purposes.
In connected speech, the joining of the end of one word to the start of the next, as in an‿apple or go‿on, so that the words sound continuous.
A simple record kept by learners of their extensive listening, noting what they listened to, for how long, what they understood and what they would like to hear next.
A short, informal check, such as a quick quiz or show of hands, that carries few or no marks and is used to confirm that learners have engaged with preparatory work and to guide the lesson.
A spoken signal that marks the large-scale organization of a lecture or talk, such as What I’d like to do today is… or Let’s now turn to… (Chaudron and Richards 1986).

A planned schedule in which the teacher marks different groups or rows of learners’ work in detail on different days, so that every notebook receives careful feedback over a cycle without overwhelming the teacher.
A language revitalization approach in which a fluent speaker, often an elder, and a learner spend many hours together using only the endangered language in everyday activities (Hinton and Hale 2001).
A learner’s own direct experience of succeeding at a task, identified by Bandura (1997) as the most powerful source of self-efficacy; visible progress records help learners notice such experiences.

Changing published or existing materials to suit a particular class, by omitting, adding, simplifying, reordering or personalizing content; for example, replacing a foreign setting in a textbook dialogue with a local one.
