An organized, growing collection of texts, tasks and resources, often gathered from the target field in ESP, that teachers can draw on and share when planning courses.

The field and practice of producing, evaluating and adapting materials for language learning, informed by research on second language acquisition; it became a recognized area of ELT in the 1990s, led by Brian Tomlinson.

The systematic judgement of the value of learning materials against explicit criteria, before, during or after use; an evaluation framework makes those criteria clear and helps teachers compare coursebooks consistently.
A teacher’s running record of the materials used or adapted for a unit, noting sources, changes made and how well they worked, so that the materials can be improved on the next run.
In listening, the process of relating the words decoded to context, prior knowledge and the speaker’s organization in order to construct an interpretation of the message (Field 2008).

A CEFR category of mediation in which a user passes on the content of a text to someone who cannot access it, for example summarizing an English notice in Kannada for a parent (Council of Europe 2020).
A CEFR category of mediation in which a user facilitates communication between people, for example across cultures or languages, acting as an intermediary (Council of Europe 2020).
A CEFR category of mediation in which a user helps others build or understand new ideas, often through collaborative group work (Council of Europe 2020).

1. In the CEFR, making meaning accessible to others, within or across languages, by relaying texts, explaining concepts or facilitating communication (Council of Europe 2020). 2. In sociocultural theory, the way tools, especially language, shape thinking and learning.
Techniques used when mediating, such as linking to previous knowledge, adapting language, amplifying a dense text or streamlining it (Council of Europe 2020).
A supportive professional relationship in which an experienced teacher guides a less experienced colleague through observation, discussion and shared reflection, rather than through evaluation alone.

A statistical method that combines the results of many studies on the same question to estimate an overall effect size; its conclusions depend on the quality of the studies included and on publication bias.
Awareness and control of one’s own thinking and learning, including planning how to approach a task, monitoring understanding and evaluating what worked.

Teaching that helps learners plan, monitor and evaluate their own listening or learning, for example through prediction, discussion of strategies and reflection after a task (Vandergrift and Goh 2012).
An approach to teaching listening that develops learners’ awareness of the listening process and their control of strategies such as predicting, monitoring and evaluating (Vandergrift and Goh 2012).

The ability to reflect on language as an object, noticing and talking about its forms and rules; multilingual learners often show this ability strongly, comparing structures across Kannada, Hindi and English.
Corrective feedback that comments on or asks about the form of an error without supplying the correct form, such as ‘Past tense?’ or ‘Is that a countable noun?’ (Lyster and Ranta 1997).

A defined set of classroom procedures based on a particular view of language and learning, such as the Audiolingual Method or the Direct Method; no single method has been shown to be best for all contexts.
A small, specific and achievable learning target, such as learning five phrases for agreeing, into which a distant goal like ‘fluency’ can be broken so that learners see steady progress.

A small spoken signal, such as so, well or right, that marks links between individual ideas in speech; for second-language listeners it usually helps less than macro-markers (Chaudron and Richards 1986).
A planned short check partway through a unit of work, used to see whether learners are on track and to adjust the remaining lessons.
A pair of words that differ in only one sound, such as ship and sheep or vest and west, used to help learners hear and produce sound contrasts that their first language may not make.
A performance slip that a learner could correct if asked, as opposed to an error, which reflects the learner’s current knowledge of the language and recurs systematically (Corder 1967).
Softening a statement or request to reduce its force or protect the relationship, for example with I think, perhaps or Could you possibly….

A research design that combines quantitative and qualitative data and analysis within one study, for example test scores together with learner interviews, so that each type of evidence helps to explain the other.

A class in which learners differ in proficiency, aptitude, pace, interests and learning needs; in practice every class is mixed-ability, and teaching responds through differentiation, tiered and open-ended tasks, and flexible grouping.
A practice examination under conditions similar to the real one, used to familiarize learners with format and timing and to identify areas that need more work.
An example text written or chosen to show the stages and language features of a target genre, which learners analyse before writing their own, for example a model formal complaint letter.
Output that a learner reformulates after a signal of difficulty from a listener, such as a clarification request; the effort may help the learner notice gaps in their own language.
Watching and listening to learners while they work, to check understanding, give help, note language for later feedback and decide when to move on.
The assumption that English is best taught through English alone, with learners’ other languages excluded (Phillipson 1992); research now supports purposeful use of the home language.
Extended spoken input from one speaker, such as a lecture or talk, which the listener cannot interrupt or negotiate, unlike conversation.
Extended speech produced by one speaker to an audience, such as a presentation or speech, which requires planning and organization; it differs from dialogic speech, in which speakers take turns.
Education in which the language of instruction is the learner’s first language or home language; India’s National Education Policy 2020 recommends it, wherever possible, until at least Grade 5.

In cognitive linguistics, the non-arbitrary link between an idiom’s literal image and its figurative meaning, as in hit the roof reflecting ‘anger is heat rising’; making this link visible can help learners remember idioms.
In genre analysis, a stage of a text that performs a recognizable communicative function, such as ‘establishing a territory’ at the start of a research article introduction (Swales 1990).
Identifying the sequence of moves in texts of a genre and the language typically used to realize each move (Swales 1990); it gives learners a map for reading and writing that genre.

A syllabus that combines several organizing strands, such as grammar, vocabulary, functions, skills and tasks, rather than following a single principle; most coursebooks and state syllabuses are of this kind.
A class, often large, in which learners are at clearly different levels of proficiency; Natalie Hess (2001) argues that such classes are the everyday setting of teaching, not an exception to it.
The mistaken belief that the ideal teacher of English is a native speaker (Phillipson 1992); expertise, training and multilingual awareness matter more than a teacher’s first language.
An ideology that treats ‘native speakers’ and their cultures as the model for English and its teaching, and so disadvantages other teachers and varieties (Holliday 2006).

The degree to which a second-language user’s speech or writing is indistinguishable from that of native speakers; it is an unrealistic and unnecessary goal for most learners compared with intelligibility.
The systematic gathering of information about why learners need English, what they must do with it, and what they already know, to guide course design and lesson planning.

A learning goal agreed jointly by learner and teacher through discussion of the learner’s needs and interests, often recorded in a learning contract, rather than simply imposed by the teacher or syllabus.
The interactional work, such as clarification requests and comprehension checks, that speakers do to resolve breakdowns in understanding; it is claimed to help acquisition (Long 1996).
Feedback that tells a learner specifically what to do next to improve, such as ‘Add a reason to each opinion’, rather than simply giving a grade or general praise.
A visual scale, often drawn on the board, that shows the acceptable noise level for an activity and lets the teacher signal when a large class needs to be quieter.
Expressing processes or qualities as nouns, as in the evaporation of water instead of water evaporates; it is a key feature of academic and scientific writing that learners need to recognize and use.
A teacher whose first language is not English; most English teachers in the world are in this position, and many bring valuable multilingual awareness and shared learning experience to the classroom.
Describes assessment that reports a learner’s performance in relation to other test takers, for example by rank or percentile, rather than against fixed criteria.
Returning to lecture or lesson notes soon after taking them, to fill gaps, summarize key points and test oneself, which strengthens understanding and memory.
Conscious attention to a feature of the input, such as a verb ending, which is argued to be necessary for it to be learnt (Schmidt 1990).
A general concept that language expresses, such as time, quantity, location or frequency; notional syllabuses organize teaching around such meanings rather than grammatical forms (Wilkins 1976).

In Universal Grammar, the parameter that determines whether a language allows subject pronouns to be omitted; Kannada and Hindi allow this, so learners may produce English sentences like ‘Is raining’.
A structured sequence for classroom observation: a pre-observation conversation to agree a focus, the observed lesson, and a post-observation conversation to reflect and plan next steps.
A focused task given to an observer, such as recording teacher questions or learner talk time, so that the observation collects specific evidence rather than general impressions.
A non-digital version of a digital activity, such as a paper quiz in place of an online one, planned so that learners without devices or connectivity are not excluded.
Three basic moves for working with a coursebook page: leave out what does not suit the class, supply what is missing and change what remains to fit learners’ level, interests and context.
Planning that speakers do while performing a task, adjusting and monitoring their speech as they go, especially when there is no time pressure.
A quick end-of-lesson writing task in which learners note, in about a minute, the most important idea they learnt or a question they still have, giving the teacher rapid feedback.
Publication of research so that anyone can read it online free of charge; it widens access for teachers without institutional subscriptions.
A licence, such as Creative Commons, that allows others to reuse, adapt and share material freely under stated conditions, such as crediting the author.
A task with more than one acceptable answer or outcome, which learners at different levels can complete to different depths, making it useful in mixed-ability classes.

In Kachru’s (1985) model of world Englishes, the countries, such as India, Nigeria and Singapore, where English was established through colonial history and has official or institutional roles alongside other languages.
The claim that producing language, especially when pushed to be precise, helps acquisition by making learners notice gaps, test hypotheses and reflect on form (Swain 1985).
Material that learners read, watch or listen to before or between lessons, as in a flipped classroom, so that class time can be used for practice and interaction.
A stage of a project or unit that learners carry out beyond the classroom, such as interviewing people or gathering information, ideally with an offline route for learners without devices.
Applying a rule beyond its proper range, as in goed or childs; such errors show that a learner is actively building a system rather than simply copying.
The deliberate use of learners’ first or home languages in English lessons, for example for explanation, comparison or mediation, as a resource rather than a failure.
Managing the speed and timing of lesson stages so that learners are neither rushed nor bored, and the lesson achieves its aim in the time available.
The position that adult second-language learners have access to some but not all of Universal Grammar, for example to principles but not to parameter values that differ from the first language.
The core, often spatial, meaning of a particle such as up or out, which cognitive linguistics uses to explain phrasal verbs; for example, up suggesting completion in eat up and fill up.
In Kumaravadivelu’s (2001) postmethod pedagogy, the principle that teaching must be sensitive to a particular group of teachers and learners in a particular institutional and social context.
A task designed for classroom use that prepares learners for real-world tasks, involving meaning-focused communication, such as a map-reading information gap.
Planned instructional strategies that deliberately draw on learners’ whole linguistic repertoire, for example discussing in Kannada before writing in English, to support learning and understanding.
Learners evaluating one another’s work against shared criteria; it develops their understanding of quality and supports their own learning, but needs training and clear rubrics.
In a large class, a learner assigned to check a partner’s or row’s work against a model answer, which reduces the teacher’s marking load.
Learners correcting one another’s errors, often after a teacher prompt; it encourages attention to form and keeps more learners involved.
Comments that learners give one another on work in progress, such as a presentation rehearsal or draft, usually guided by criteria or sentence frames.
Teachers observing one another’s lessons for mutual learning rather than evaluation, usually with an agreed focus and a follow-up conversation.
The evaluation of a research article by independent experts before publication; it is a key marker of quality when teachers judge research sources.
Arranging for learners to teach one another, for example explaining a point to a partner, structured so that both partners benefit.
A structured arrangement in which one learner tutors another; research suggests that tutors often gain as much as tutees when roles are well organized (Topping 2005).
Bahrick’s (1984) term for knowledge that, after an initial period of forgetting, remains stable in memory for decades, such as some school foreign-language vocabulary.
An approach to teaching literature that uses texts to engage learners’ emotions, experiences and personal responses, aiming at development as readers and people (Carter and Long 1991).
Adapting activities so that learners use the target language to talk about their own lives, opinions and experiences, which makes practice more meaningful and memorable.
The smallest unit of sound that distinguishes meaning in a language, such as /p/ and /b/ in pin and bin.
A chart showing the phonemic symbols for the sounds of English, usually arranged by place and manner of articulation, used to teach and refer to pronunciation.
A method of teaching reading by linking letters and letter groups to the sounds they represent, so that learners can decode and blend unfamiliar words.

A small-scale trial run of a research study, carried out to test instruments such as questionnaires, and procedures such as timing, before the main study; problems found are fixed before full data collection.
Trying out new materials or a test with a small group before full use, in order to identify problems and revise them.
A test used at the start of a course to place learners in the group or level best suited to their current proficiency.
Time given before a task for learners to prepare what they will say or write; research links it to greater fluency and complexity in performance.

A stage, common at intermediate level, when learners feel they are no longer making progress despite effort; it can be addressed with new challenges, micro-goals and visible progress records (Richards 2008).
Learning through purposeful play, such as games, songs, role play and movement, especially with young learners; it is emphasized in NEP 2020 for the foundational stage.
The functions on an audio or video player, such as pause, replay and slowing down, that learners can use strategically to make listening manageable.
The recognition that English exists in many legitimate varieties, such as Indian English, rather than as a single standard owned by native speakers.
A language with several interacting centres, each providing a national variety with its own norms, as English has in Britain, the USA, India and elsewhere.
The interconnected set of languages and language knowledge a person has, which they can draw on flexibly when communicating or learning (Council of Europe 2020).
The perspective from which a story is told, such as first-person or third-person narration; discussing it helps learners interpret literary texts.
The ways language users show consideration for others and manage social relationships, such as through forms of address, indirectness and hedging.
A linguistic means of reducing threat to the listener’s face, such as indirect requests or hedges, as described by Brown and Levinson (1987).
A purposeful collection of a learner’s work over time, often with reflections, which shows progress and supports assessment for learning.
In cooperative learning, a condition in which group members need one another to succeed, so that each member’s contribution matters (Johnson and Johnson 1989).

The beneficial effect of a test on teaching and learning, for example when including a speaking component in a school examination encourages teachers to give learners regular speaking practice in class.
In Kumaravadivelu’s (2001) postmethod pedagogy, the principle that teaching should draw on learners’ sociopolitical awareness and identity, and aim at social change as well as language learning.
The discussion after an observed lesson in which the observer and the teacher reflect together on the evidence collected, rather than on general impressions, and agree realistic next steps.
Kumaravadivelu’s (1994) term for the situation in which teachers look for an alternative to method rather than an alternative method, building their own principled practice.

An approach to teaching based on the postmethod condition and the parameters of particularity, practicality and possibility, which positions teachers as theorizers of their own practice (Kumaravadivelu 2001).
A word that follows a noun to show relations such as place or direction, as in Kannada and Hindi, where English uses a preposition before the noun; comparing these orders helps learners.
Chomsky’s argument that the language children hear is insufficient to explain the complex grammar they acquire, which suggests some innate knowledge of language.
See presentation, practice, production.

1. In assessment, whether a test is feasible given time, cost and resources. 2. In Kumaravadivelu’s (2001) postmethod pedagogy, the principle that teachers should theorize from their practice and practise what they theorize.
A rehearsal of a presentation or performance before the real event, often with peer feedback, to build confidence and improve delivery.
Teacher development that takes place within daily teaching, such as through lesson study, peer observation or classroom inquiry, rather than in one-off workshops.
The supervised teaching practice component of a teacher education programme, in which trainees teach real classes with guidance and feedback.

A publication written mainly for teachers that reports classroom-based work and practical ideas in accessible language, such as ELT Journal or English Teaching Professional, as distinct from a purely academic research journal.
The knowledge teachers build from their own classroom experience and reflection, about particular learners, contexts and what works; it complements, and can challenge, findings from formal research.
Research that teachers carry out on their own classrooms to understand and improve practice, such as action research or exploratory practice.

The inability to understand or convey intended meaning because language, though grammatically correct, is inappropriate to the context or relationship, such as an overly direct request to a senior officer (Thomas 1983).

The study of how meaning depends on context, speakers’ intentions and social relationships, including speech acts, politeness and implied meaning; for example, how ‘It’s cold in here’ can function as a request.
The discussion before an observed lesson in which the teacher and observer agree the lesson’s aims and the focus of observation.
Initial teacher education undertaken before a teacher begins employment, such as a D.El.Ed or B.Ed programme, combining coursework in subject and pedagogy with a supervised practicum.
In task-based teaching, the stage before the main task that introduces the topic, activates vocabulary and may include planning or modelling.
Time given before a task for learners to plan the content and language of their performance; research suggests it tends to increase fluency and complexity, with more mixed effects on accuracy.

A publication that charges authors fees but provides little or no genuine peer review or editorial quality control; teachers submitting or citing research should check a journal’s credentials before trusting it.
An affix added to the beginning of a word to change its meaning, such as un- in unhappy or re- in rewrite.
A preposition that shows where something is, such as in, on, under, next to or opposite; in English it comes before the noun, unlike the postpositions of Kannada or Hindi.
A version of a research paper shared publicly before peer review; it may be useful but should be read with caution.
In ESP course design, the analysis of learners’ current language abilities, resources and learning situation at the start of a course.
Nervousness about speaking in front of an audience, which can hinder performance and can be reduced through rehearsal and support.
A lesson sequence in which the teacher presents a language item, learners practise it in controlled activities, and then use it more freely in production.
Combining techniques from different methods on the basis of a coherent rationale suited to the context, rather than mixing them at random.
Chomsky’s (1981) model of Universal Grammar, in which universal principles are shared by all languages and parameters are set differently in each language.
Speech addressed to oneself to guide thinking and action, such as muttering while working out a problem; in Vygotskian theory it helps learners regulate their learning.

In Littlewood’s (1999) distinction, autonomy in which learners set their own direction, goals and methods, as opposed to reactive autonomy, where they organize their learning within a direction set by others.
Assessment of how learners work over the course of a project, such as planning, collaboration and problem-solving, rather than only the final product.
Evaluation of how learning is progressing during a course or contract, rather than only at the end, so that goals and methods can be adjusted.
An approach to teaching writing that focuses on the stages writers go through, such as planning, drafting, revising and editing, with feedback from teacher or peers between drafts.
Assessment of the final outcome of a project or task, such as a poster, report or presentation, against clear criteria.
Speaking and writing, the skills in which learners produce language, as opposed to the receptive skills of listening and reading.
Holding several theories together in planning and teaching, rather than choosing one, so that their differences lead to a richer, more balanced practice.

The continuing learning and growth of teachers throughout their careers, through training, reflection, collaboration, observation and classroom research; it is most effective when sustained and linked to daily practice.
A record kept by learners during a project, noting what they did, what they learnt and what they will do next, often used in assessment.
The final product of a project, such as a poster, video, report or presentation, which gives the work purpose and an audience.
An approach in which learners work over an extended period on a project that produces a real outcome, integrating language skills with research and collaboration.
In cooperative learning, face-to-face interaction in which group members help, encourage and explain to one another (Johnson and Johnson 1989).
1. In error correction, a move that pushes the learner to self-correct, such as a clarification request or metalinguistic clue. 2. In generative AI, the instruction or question typed to the system.
The most typical member of a category, such as robin for ‘bird’; cognitive linguistics shows that language categories have central and peripheral members.
The statistical and theoretical process of gathering evidence that a test measures what it claims to measure consistently and fairly.
The tendency for studies with positive or significant results to be published more often than those with null results, which can distort the research picture.
Output that learners are pushed to make more accurate, precise or appropriate, for example by a request to reformulate; producing it may help them notice gaps and promote acquisition (Swain 1985).
Research that gathers and interprets non-numerical data, such as interviews, observations, diaries or classroom recordings, to understand experiences, perspectives and meanings in depth.
Research that gathers and analyses numerical data, such as test scores or survey responses, using statistics to measure variables, compare groups or test relationships between them.
An experimental study that compares groups that were not randomly assigned, such as two existing sections in a school; it is common in classroom research but weaker in ruling out other explanations.

A positive, trusting relationship between teacher and learners, built through respect, warmth, fairness and genuine interest in learners, which encourages participation and willingness to take risks in English.
How quickly a learner progresses, as distinct from ultimate attainment; older learners often learn faster at first, though younger starters may reach higher levels in the long run.
The consistency of scores given by different raters, or by the same rater at different times, to the same performance; it is improved by calibration and double-marking.

Autonomy in which learners organize their own work towards goals the teacher has set, before they set goals themselves (Littlewood 1999). It is often the natural first step, for example learners choosing which graded reader to use for a teacher-set reading target.

How easy a text is to read for a particular group of learners, shaped by vocabulary, sentence length, organization, topic familiarity and layout. Formulas give a rough estimate, but a teacher’s judgement of the class remains essential.

An approach to literature that treats meaning as made in the interaction between reader and text, so learners’ personal responses become the starting point for discussion (Rosenblatt 1978). A class might share reactions to a Kannada or English poem before analysing it.

A simple record in which learners note what they have read, for how long and a brief response. It supports extensive reading and self-study, and helps the teacher monitor quantity and enjoyment without formal testing.

The classroom skill of noticing, moment to moment, how learners are responding, through faces, posture, noise and task progress, and adjusting pace, instructions or activity accordingly. It is part of the largely invisible craft of teaching.

People beyond the teacher who will genuinely read, hear or use learners’ work, such as parents, a headteacher, SMC members or another class. Writing or presenting for a real audience raises motivation and makes the task more purposeful.

A task that closely mirrors something people actually do outside the classroom, such as booking a ticket, writing a complaint or following directions. It contrasts with a pedagogic task, which is designed for learning but may not occur in everyday life.

In a spoken or written argument, the statement that explains why a claim should be accepted. Learners are taught the simple structure claim–reason–evidence, for example ‘Schools should have libraries because…’, followed by an example.

A task in which learners derive new information from given information through inference, deduction or practical reasoning, such as working out a timetable from clues. The term comes from Prabhu’s Bangalore project (Prabhu 1987).

In argument and debate, a response that challenges or answers the opposing side’s claims. Toulmin (1958) included rebuttals in his model of argument; in class, a mini-debate can give each team a short, timed rebuttal turn.

Corrective feedback in which the teacher reformulates all or part of a learner’s incorrect utterance correctly, without explicitly signalling the error (Lyster and Ranta 1997). For example, learner: ‘He go yesterday’; teacher: ‘Oh, he went yesterday?’

The language skills of listening and reading, through which learners receive and understand language, as distinct from the productive skills of speaking and writing. Receptive ability is usually larger than, and often retained longer than, productive ability.

Planned reintroduction of previously taught language in new contexts and activities so that it is met, retrieved and used repeatedly over time. Recycling helps vocabulary and grammar move from recognition towards fluent, confident use.

A cohesive device in which a word such as a pronoun, demonstrative or comparative points to something mentioned elsewhere in the text (Halliday and Hasan 1976). In ‘Ravi lost his bag. He found it later’, he and it are reference items.

The sequence of words in a text that refer to the same person or thing, such as a name followed by pronouns and synonyms. Tracing reference chains helps learners follow texts and repair ambiguous pronouns in their own writing.

A large, general collection of texts used as a benchmark against which a smaller corpus, such as learners’ essays, is compared to show which patterns are distinctive or unusual, for example learners’ frequent ‘discuss about’.

The formal process of passing concerns about a learner to a specialist, such as a special educator, counsellor or medical professional, for further assessment and support. Classroom support should continue while the referral is being made.

The process of thinking back on one’s learning or teaching in order to understand it and decide what to do next. For learners, it may take the form of a short reflection slip attached to a piece of portfolio work.

Thinking about and adjusting one’s practice while it is happening, such as changing an activity mid-lesson when learners are confused (Schön 1983). It contrasts with reflection-on-action, which takes place after the event.

Looking back on practice after the event in order to understand it and plan improvements, for example writing notes after a lesson or discussing it with a colleague (Schön 1983). It complements reflection-in-action.

A model of professional education in which received knowledge from research and experiential knowledge from practice are brought together through cycles of practice and reflection (Wallace 1991). It contrasts with the craft and applied science models.

Variation in language according to the situation of use, especially the subject matter, the relationship between participants and the channel of communication. A learner writes differently in a WhatsApp message to a friend and a leave letter to the headteacher.

A mediation strategy in which a speaker or writer adjusts the formality, technicality or style of a message for a new audience, for example explaining a formal circular from the school office in simple everyday language for parents.

The consistency of a test’s results: whether the same learner would get a similar score on another day, with another marker or on another version of the test. Clear marking criteria and marker training improve reliability.

Repeating a research study, exactly or with planned changes, to see whether its findings hold in another setting or with other participants. Replication is essential before a single study’s results are treated as reliable evidence for practice.

The stage of the task cycle in which groups prepare and present an account of how they did the task and what they decided or found, usually to the whole class. Planning the report pushes learners towards more accurate, public language (Willis 1996).

A verb used to introduce or attribute the words or ideas of others, such as argue, claim, suggest or note. In academic writing, the choice of reporting verb signals the writer’s stance towards the source.

The way people, places, cultures and languages are portrayed, or left out, in teaching materials. Critical review asks whose lives and perspectives a coursebook presents as normal, and whether Indian learners can see their own worlds in it.

The repeated sequence of steps in action research: identifying a problem, planning an intervention, acting, observing and collecting evidence, and reflecting, which then leads to a revised plan and a new cycle.

A dated record kept by a teacher-researcher during an enquiry, noting observations, decisions, learner responses and developing interpretations. It is a source of evidence in its own right and supports honest reflection on the research process.

In lesson study, a lesson planned in detail by a group of teachers, taught by one while the others observe learners’ responses, and then revised and often retaught (Stigler and Hiebert 1999; Lewis 2002).

The procedures used to collect and analyse evidence, such as experiments, surveys, interviews, observation and case studies. Understanding their strengths and limits helps teachers judge what a study can and cannot show about classrooms.

A collaboration between teachers and academic researchers or teacher-education institutions, ideally reciprocal, in which both sides shape the questions and benefit from the findings. A DIET and a group of schools might jointly study a reading programme.

A clear, focused question that a piece of research sets out to answer, such as ‘Does five minutes of daily pair talk increase how much my Class 7 learners speak in English?’ A good one is specific and answerable with available evidence.

The distance between what research findings suggest and what actually happens in classrooms, caused partly by inaccessible publications and partly by research that ignores classroom realities. Practitioner research and partnerships aim to narrow it.

The learner skill of judging self-study materials, such as apps, videos and books, for level, purpose and quality before using them. It is an important part of learner autonomy and extends earlier strategy training.

Learning by actively recalling information from memory, for example through self-quizzing or flashcards, rather than rereading it. Retrieval strengthens long-term retention (Roediger and Karpicke 2006), especially when spread over time.
Mentoring in which a less experienced or younger teacher supports a more senior colleague in an area of their own expertise, such as digital tools, while also learning from the relationship.

A week built into a scheme of work for revisiting and consolidating earlier units rather than introducing new material. Review weeks protect time for recycling, catching up and assessment across the school year.

In process writing, making changes to the content, ideas and organization of a draft, as distinct from editing, which corrects spelling, grammar and punctuation. Learners often edit but do not yet revise.

A short record kept with teaching materials in which teachers note, after each use, what worked, what did not and what to change. It turns materials development into a continuous, shared improvement process.

Organized efforts to reverse language shift and increase the use of an endangered language, for example through community classes, mother-tongue schooling, recording elders and creating new materials. Many draw on familiar language-teaching methods.

A card giving a learner the information needed to take part in a role-play, such as who they are, what they want and any constraints. Different cards for each partner create an information or opinion gap.

A speaking activity in which learners take on roles, often with role cards, and act out a situation such as a shop conversation or a meeting with a doctor. It lets learners rehearse language for situations beyond the classroom.

A scoring guide that sets out the criteria for assessing a piece of work and describes performance at each level. Shared in advance, a rubric makes expectations clear and supports self-assessment and peer assessment.

Temporary support that helps learners do what they could not yet do alone, gradually withdrawn as competence grows (Wood, Bruner and Ross 1976). Examples include sentence frames, modelling, visual prompts and guiding questions.

A planned reduction in support across a unit of work, from heavy scaffolding in early lessons to independent performance by the end. It makes the gradual handover of responsibility to learners visible in the unit plan.
Reading quickly to find specific information, such as a date, name or figure, without reading the whole text. Looking up a train time in a timetable is a typical scanning task.
A term’s or year’s teaching plan that turns a syllabus into a sequence of units, with time allocations, review weeks and assessment points. It sits between the syllabus and individual lesson plans.

Reducing the planned outcome of a project to something achievable when time or resources run short, rather than abandoning it. A class planning a full magazine might produce a single-page newsletter instead.

Deciding what a test score does and does not show about a learner’s ability. A high exam score may not prove real-world performance, so scores must be read in the light of what the test actually measured.

The study of how people learn languages other than their first, and the processes involved. The acronym SLA refers both to the process and to the research field, which informs many teaching decisions.

The loss of second-language ability after use or study stops, for example when school English is little used after leaving school. Productive skills and less frequent vocabulary are usually lost first; receptive knowledge tends to last longer.

An obstacle to technology use that lies in teachers’ beliefs about teaching and learning, confidence and school culture, rather than in devices, connectivity or time, which are first-order barriers (Ertmer and Ottenbreit-Leftwich 2010).

The individual sounds of a language, its consonants and vowels, as distinct from suprasegmental features such as stress and intonation. Examples include the difference between /v/ and /w/ or /ɪ/ and /iː/.

Listening for particular information while ignoring the rest, such as noting only the key dates in a lecture or the platform number in an announcement. It is an important strategy for coping with long or fast spoken texts.

A room or space with organized learning materials, such as graded readers, audio, worksheets and answer keys, which learners use independently to work on their own goals, often with advice available (Gardner and Miller 1999).

Learners judging their own performance or progress against criteria, for example with ‘can do’ statements or a checklist. It builds awareness, responsibility and autonomy, and gives the teacher useful information.

A learner correcting their own error, often after a prompt from the teacher such as a repeated word, a questioning look or a gesture. Self-correction encourages learners to notice and apply what they already know.

A person’s belief in their ability to succeed at a particular task (Bandura 1977). Learners with higher self-efficacy in English persist longer and take more risks; achievable tasks and specific praise help to build it.

Learners keeping track of their own learning, such as progress towards goals, recurring errors or time spent, and adjusting their strategies accordingly. An error log is a common self-monitoring tool.

Learning in which learners plan, monitor and evaluate their own learning, managing goals, strategies, motivation and time (Zimmerman 2000). Also called self-regulation, it is developed through goal-setting, self-monitoring and reflection.
Learners evaluating their own performance against criteria, for example watching a phone recording of their presentation with a checklist and identifying one strength and one thing to improve.

Learning that learners do on their own outside class, such as reading, listening, vocabulary review or practice with apps. With limited class hours in most Indian schools, well-taught self-study strategies greatly extend learning time.
The extent to which learners have the skills, access, habits and confidence to learn independently, often checked with a short checklist before a blended or flipped model is introduced.

A teacher’s own developing understanding of how learning happens, which guides classroom decisions (Prabhu 1990). Prabhu argued it matters more than any one method, and that it stays alive through reflection and engagement with ideas.
A period in development when learning a particular aspect of language is easier and more successful, but after which it remains possible. It is a weaker version of the critical period idea.

The pattern of strong and weak syllables across an utterance, in which content words carrying key meaning are stressed and many function words are reduced. It gives English its rhythm and highlights important information.
Words and phrases that show the structure of a talk or text, such as ‘First…’, ‘Moving on to…’ and ‘To sum up…’. Speakers use them to guide listeners; listeners use them to follow the organization.

An extended activity in which learners act within a realistic, structured situation, such as a village panchayat meeting or a news studio, often keeping their own views and drawing on information provided.

A presentation format in which several groups present at the same time to different small audiences, then rotate. It gives every group more speaking time and more listeners than whole-class presentations in a large class.

Combining two or more language skills in one activity or sequence, as in real life, for example reading a notice, discussing it and writing a reply. Integration makes practice more meaningful and helps skills support each other.

Hiring English teachers on the basis of qualifications, language proficiency and teaching skill rather than native-speaker status. It is presented as a fairer, more ethical alternative to native-speakerism in recruitment.

The four language skills of listening, speaking, reading and writing, through which language is used. They are usually planned alongside, and distinguished from, the language systems of grammar, vocabulary, pronunciation and discourse.

The proportion of attention given to each of the four skills across a unit or course. Many textbook-led courses overemphasize reading and writing, so teachers plan to restore time for listening and speaking.
A syllabus organized around language skills and sub-skills, such as skimming, note-taking or giving a presentation, rather than grammar points or topics.
Reading quickly to get the general idea or gist of a text, without attending to detail, for example glancing through a newspaper article to see what it is about before deciding whether to read it.

The CEFR’s view of the language learner as a person acting in society with a plurilingual repertoire, in which languages interact rather than being kept separate (Council of Europe 2020). It underpins the CEFR’s mediation scales.

In cooperative learning, the interpersonal skills needed for group work, such as listening, taking turns, encouraging others and disagreeing politely. Johnson and Johnson (1989) argue these must be taught explicitly, not assumed.

Knowledge of how to use language appropriately in different social contexts, including politeness, register and social conventions (Canale and Swain 1980). Knowing how to address a principal as against a classmate is one example.

Spreading study or practice over several sessions with gaps between them, rather than concentrating it in one block. Spaced practice leads to better long-term retention than cramming the night before an examination.
Reviewing items, especially vocabulary, at gradually increasing intervals, just as they are about to be forgotten. Many flashcard apps schedule reviews automatically using this principle.

A difference in the way a person processes information that affects particular aspects of learning, such as reading, spelling or number, without reflecting general intelligence. Dyslexia is the most familiar example.

Praise that names exactly what a learner did well, such as ‘You used three linking words in that paragraph’, rather than a general ‘Good’. It tells learners what to repeat and builds realistic confidence.

Assessment that reflects the contexts and tasks of learners’ target situation, such as a nurse’s shift handover or an engineer’s report (Douglas 2000). It is used in English for Specific Purposes courses.

An utterance considered as an action, such as requesting, apologizing, promising or complaining (Austin 1962; Searle 1969). The same act can be performed in more or less direct ways, and appropriateness varies across cultures.

Technology that converts spoken language into text or responds to spoken input, used in dictation tools, voice assistants and pronunciation apps. Accuracy can vary with accent, so its feedback should be treated with care.

A curriculum in which topics and language are revisited repeatedly over time, each time at a greater level of depth or complexity (Bruner 1960). The past tense might be met first in simple stories, later in narratives and reports.

A recognizable type of spoken interaction with a social purpose and typical stages, such as storytelling, service encounters or gossip (Eggins and Slade 1997). Mapping its stages gives learners a structure for unpredictable talk.

Grammatical features typical of conversation rather than writing, such as ellipsis, heads and tails, discourse markers and vague language (Carter and McCarthy 2006). Textbooks often underrepresent it.

In genre-based teaching, one of the typical functional steps through which a genre achieves its purpose, such as the orientation, complication and resolution of a narrative. Teachers analyse stages with learners before they write.

Anyone with an interest in a course or its outcomes, such as learners, parents, teachers, employers, subject specialists or administrators. In course design, stakeholders are consulted during needs analysis.

The importance of a test’s consequences for the people involved. High-stakes tests, such as board examinations, affect futures and so tend to produce stronger washback than low-stakes classroom quizzes.
A statistical estimate of how far an observed test score is likely to differ from a learner’s ‘true’ score because of measurement error. It reminds users that a score is a band, not an exact point.

The belief that one idealized, uniform variety of a language is inherently correct and superior, and that other varieties are deficient (Lippi-Green 1997). In ELT it can lead to devaluing Indian English and learners’ own speech.

The distinction between what teachers say they believe about teaching and the beliefs visible in their actual classroom practice (Phipps and Borg 2009). The gap is common, reflects constraints such as examinations and time, and is useful for reflection.

A fixed, oversimplified generalization about a group of people, applied to every member. In intercultural teaching, learners examine stereotypes, including those in materials, and learn to see individuals and diversity within cultures.

A research method in which participants watch a recording of their own actions, such as a lesson, and explain what they were thinking at particular moments (Gass and Mackey 2000). It helps reveal teachers’ tacit decision-making.

Activities chosen to manage young learners’ energy: stirrers, such as action songs or running dictation, raise energy; settlers, such as colouring or story listening, calm the class. Teachers alternate them across a lesson.
The ability to use verbal and non-verbal strategies to keep communication going when knowledge runs short, such as paraphrasing, asking for clarification or using gesture (Canale and Swain 1980).

A syllabus organized around grammatical structures, sequenced roughly from simpler to more complex, such as the present simple before the present perfect. It was long dominant in Indian English textbooks.

The principle that grammatical rules operate on hierarchical structures, not on the linear order of words. Children forming questions such as ‘Is the boy who is singing happy?’ appear to respect it without instruction (Crain and Nakayama 1987).
See student talking time (STT).
The proportion of lesson time in which learners, rather than the teacher, are speaking. Pair and group work, wait time and genuine questions all increase STT, giving learners more practice.

A deliberate technique learners use to learn more effectively on their own, such as retrieval practice, spaced review, keeping a vocabulary notebook or planning study time. Such strategies need to be taught explicitly.

The study of style in texts using linguistic analysis, examining how choices of words, grammar, sound and structure create meaning and effect, particularly in literature. It links language study and literary response.
An expert in the learners’ professional or academic field, such as a nurse, engineer or lawyer, with whom an ESP teacher collaborates on needs analysis, materials and assessment.

A viewing routine in which learners watch a clip without subtitles, then with English subtitles, then without again, so that the subtitled viewing supports understanding and the final viewing tests listening.

A situation in which learning a second language leads to loss or weakening of the first, often when the first language has low status (Lambert 1974). It contrasts with additive bilingualism, where the first language is maintained.
A morpheme added to the end of a word to change its meaning or word class, such as -ness in kindness or -ful in helpful. Teaching common suffixes helps learners work out and build word families.

Assessment at the end of a unit, term or course to measure and report what learners have achieved, such as an end-of-term examination. It contrasts with formative assessment, which informs ongoing teaching.
Adding materials or activities to a coursebook to fill its gaps, for example extra listening and speaking tasks for a textbook that focuses mainly on reading and grammar.

Features of pronunciation that extend over more than one sound, such as word stress, sentence stress, rhythm, intonation and connected speech. They often matter more for intelligibility than individual sounds.

The difference between adding diverse faces or names to otherwise unchanged materials (surface diversity) and reshaping content, perspectives and settings to centre other lives (deep diversity), for example setting a text in Mysuru during Dasara.

A regular period in which everyone, including the teacher, reads self-chosen material silently without tasks or tests. It builds reading habits and fluency, and is often used within an extensive reading programme.

The genre-based approach developed in Australian schools from the 1980s by J. R. Martin, Joan Rothery, David Rose and colleagues, drawing on systemic functional linguistics to make powerful school genres explicit (Martin and Rose 2008).

A specification of what is to be taught in a course and, often, in what order, such as grammar points, functions, skills, topics or tasks. It is narrower than a curriculum and broader than a scheme of work.

The deliberate combination of two or more syllabus types, such as topic, task, skills and structural strands, within a unit plan, recorded so that the unit’s main organizing principle and supporting strands are clear.

A consistent deviation from the target language that reflects a learner’s current rule, as distinct from a random slip or mistake (Corder 1967). A learner who always writes ‘goed’ and ‘buyed’ is applying a rule.

A research review that searches for, selects and appraises all relevant studies on a question using explicit, replicable methods, often combining results statistically. It gives stronger evidence than a single study.
The language systems of grammar, vocabulary, pronunciation and discourse, which underlie the four skills. Planning with both skills and systems in view helps teachers balance a lesson or unit.

A belief about teaching that a teacher holds without being fully aware of it, often formed through their own schooling. Such beliefs shape classroom decisions and can be surfaced through reflection, observation and discussion.

Knowledge that people use in practice but find hard to put into words (Polanyi 1966). Much of teachers’ expertise, such as knowing when to move on, is tacit and can be explored through stimulated recall.
The real-world context in which learners will need to use English, such as a workplace, college course or travel. Describing it clarifies what learners must be able to do and guides course planning.

The part of needs analysis that identifies what learners will need to do in English in their target situation, including tasks, texts and skills (Hutchinson and Waters 1987). It is paired with present-situation analysis.

A meaning-focused activity in which learners use language to achieve a non-linguistic outcome, drawing on their own resources (Ellis 2003). Planning a class trip within a budget is a task; a drill of pre-specified sentences is not.

The cognitive demands a task makes on learners, shaped by features such as the number of elements, reasoning required and time pressure (Robinson 2001). Complexity can be raised or lowered to sequence tasks.
The central phase of a task-based lesson, in which learners do the task, plan a report and present it to the class (Willis 1996). It is preceded by a pre-task and followed by a language focus.

Design characteristics of a task, such as the type of information gap, complexity and planning time, that research links to learner performance in fluency, accuracy and complexity (Skehan 1998; Ellis 2003).

Adjusting the difficulty of a task, rather than the text, to suit learners’ level, for example asking lower-level learners to find three facts and more advanced learners to evaluate the writer’s argument using the same text.

The concrete result that a task produces, such as a completed map, a decision, a list or a poster. A clear outcome gives the task a purpose and allows teacher and learners to judge whether it was achieved.
Asking learners to do the same or a similar task again, often with a different partner, so that freed attention can go to fluency, accuracy or complexity (Bygate 2001).
A syllabus organized around a sequence of tasks rather than grammar points or topics, with language arising from task performance. Tasks are graded by complexity and familiarity.
What teachers know, believe and think, and how this relates to what they do in the classroom (Borg 2003). It is shaped by schooling, training, experience and context.

The tendency for a teacher’s expectations of learners to influence their performance, through differences in attention, questioning and feedback (Rosenthal and Jacobson 1968). Low expectations of ‘weak’ learners can become self-fulfilling.

The knowledge, skill and judgement that develop as teachers gain experience and reflect on it, allowing them to read situations quickly and respond flexibly. Experience alone does not guarantee expertise; reflection and learning are essential.

How teachers see themselves as professionals, shaped by their histories, language backgrounds, communities and work. For non-native-speaking teachers of English in India, a confident identity is an important professional resource.
A group of teachers who meet regularly to learn together, share practice, observe each other and try out new ideas, such as a school or cluster-level group supported by a DIET.
The proportion of lesson time in which the teacher is speaking. Excessive TTT reduces learners’ practice, though well-judged teacher talk also provides valuable input.
A teacher’s personal, reasoned set of beliefs about how languages are learned and how best to teach them, which guides classroom decisions and develops with experience and reflection.
A short written account of a teacher’s beliefs about learning and teaching, with examples from practice. It is often used for reflection, professional portfolios and job applications.
Narrowing teaching to the content and formats of an examination, often at the expense of wider language skills. It is a common form of negative washback in high-stakes systems.
The genre-based cycle of building the field, deconstructing model texts, joint construction and independent construction, with support gradually reduced (Martin and Rose 2008).
See virtual exchange.
A change in how a test is given, such as extra time, large print, a reader or a separate room, that removes a barrier for a learner with a particular need without changing what the test measures.

Systematic unfairness in a test that disadvantages a group of test takers for reasons unrelated to the ability being measured, for example reading passages that assume familiarity with urban or foreign contexts.
The principle that a test gives all test takers an equal opportunity to show their ability, through unbiased content, appropriate accommodations, consistent administration and just use of scores.

The structure and task types of a test, such as multiple choice, gap-fill, essay or oral interview, and their timing. Learners benefit from familiarity with a format, but this should not replace skill development.

A document setting out what a test measures and how, including its purpose, test takers, content, task types, marking and weighting. It guides test writers and helps ensure consistency across versions.
Commercial coaching centres, books and courses that prepare candidates for high-stakes tests. It can help familiarity but raises fairness concerns, since access depends on ability to pay.
A lesson sequence in which learners first attempt a task to reveal what they know, the teacher then teaches the language they need, and learners attempt a similar task again.
A shared, organized collection of texts, graded and labelled by level, topic and genre, which teachers build and draw on for teaching. A staffroom text bank can include a permissions checklist.
The percentage of running words in a text that a reader knows. Research suggests about 98 per cent coverage is needed for comfortable unassisted reading (Hu and Nation 2000).
An approach to materials design in which an engaging text is chosen first and the language focus emerges from it, rather than a language point determining the text (Tomlinson 2011).
In systemic functional linguistics, the starting point of a clause, which sets up what the clause is about (Halliday 1985). Choosing themes well helps writers guide readers through a text.
The ability to understand and critically evaluate theories and research claims in language teaching, including how research is done and what it can show. It differs from simply collecting techniques.

Recognizing that several theories, such as cognitive, sociocultural and usage-based accounts, each explain part of language learning, and drawing on them thoughtfully rather than committing to only one.

The relationship between theories of language learning and teachers’ classroom decisions. Teachers make the link by testing ideas against their experience and by using theory to explain what they observe.

A cooperative structure in which learners think about a question individually, discuss it with a partner and then share ideas with the class (Lyman 1981). It increases participation and gives learners time to prepare.

Kachru’s model of English worldwide, with the Inner Circle (e.g. the UK), the Outer Circle where English is a second or official language (e.g. India) and the Expanding Circle (e.g. China) (Kachru 1985).
A task prepared at several levels of challenge on the same content, so that learners of different abilities can all work on the same topic, for example three versions of a reading task.
A line diagram showing past, present and future, used to clarify the time reference of verb forms, such as the difference between the past simple and present perfect.
Understanding a text by drawing on background knowledge, context and expectations about the topic and genre, rather than decoding word by word. It works together with bottom-up processing.
Peer review in which learners are first taught how to give useful feedback, through modelling, criteria and practice. Training improves the quality of feedback and revisions (Min 2006).

Using one’s full linguistic repertoire, across named languages, to make meaning and learn (García and Li Wei 2014). In class, learners might discuss a text in Kannada or Hindi before writing in English.
Conveying the meaning of a text from one language to another. In the classroom it is distinguished from broader mediation and can be a valuable, purposeful activity rather than a shortcut to avoid.

Using several sources, methods or perspectives to check findings, for example combining learner interviews, employer views and document analysis in needs analysis, or observation and learner work in action research.
See teacher talking time (TTT).
A quick routine in which learners turn to a neighbour and discuss a question for a minute or two. It gives everyone a chance to speak, even in large classes with fixed benches.
Tracking two strands of learning, such as language and subject content, or process and product, side by side, often on a simple tracking sheet. It keeps both visible when judging learner progress.
A task in which each participant holds information the other needs, so that both must exchange information to complete it. It generates more negotiation of meaning than a one-way task.

A pattern in which learners use a form correctly, then produce errors, and later use it correctly again, such as went, then goed, then went. It signals rule formation, not forgetting (Lightbown and Spada 2013).
The final level of proficiency a learner reaches in a second language after long exposure. Research on age often compares ultimate attainment with the rate of learning.
The overall goal of a unit of work, stating what learners should be able to do by its end. Each lesson aim should move learners closer to it.
A coherent block of lessons, usually over several weeks, built around a theme, text or outcome, with aims, a sequence of activities and assessment.
A written plan for a unit of work, setting out its aims, syllabus blend, lesson sequence, assessment checkpoints and final task or product.
The topic that holds a unit of work together, chosen to be rich enough to support discourse and pragmatics work as well as vocabulary and grammar.

A framework for planning lessons that are accessible to all learners from the start, by offering multiple means of engagement, representation and action and expression, rather than adapting afterwards for individuals.
Chomsky’s proposal that humans have innate principles common to all languages, which constrain and guide language acquisition (Chomsky 1965). Its role in second language learning remains debated.
An approach, also called Dogme, that reduces reliance on published materials and technology, building lessons from the learners’ own talk and emergent language (Meddings and Thornbury 2009).
A learner’s immediate response to corrective feedback, such as repeating or correcting the form (Lyster and Ranta 1997). Uptake shows that feedback was noticed, but does not in itself prove learning.

The view that language knowledge is built from the expressions people actually meet and use, through general cognitive abilities such as pattern-finding (Tomasello 2003). It emphasizes frequency, exposure and meaningful use.
The extent to which a test measures what it claims to measure and supports the decisions made with its scores. A speaking test that only checks written grammar has low validity.
A claim made by a company about the effectiveness of its product, such as an app or platform. Teachers should distinguish vendor claims from independent research evidence and test them locally.

Online, sustained collaboration between learners in different places, often in different countries, to develop language and intercultural skills. Also called telecollaboration, it can link Indian classes with partner schools elsewhere.
The positive cycle in which enjoyment of reading leads to more reading, which leads to greater ease and further enjoyment (Nuttall 2005). It contrasts with the vicious circle of the weak reader.
Pictures, charts, objects, slides or board drawings used to support communication and understanding. In presentations they should support, not replace, what the speaker says.
The proportion of words in a text that a reader knows, used to judge whether a text suits a learner’s level. Extensive reading generally needs very high coverage, around 98 per cent (Nation 2006).
The pause a teacher allows after asking a question before calling on a learner or answering it. Longer wait time leads to more and better responses (Rowe 1986).

The effect of a test on teaching and learning, which may be positive or negative (Alderson and Wall 1993). Board examinations that test only reading and writing often lead to neglect of listening and speaking.
The reduced pronunciation of a function word when unstressed, often with the vowel /ə/, such as /tə/ for to in ‘I want to go’. Weak forms are essential for natural rhythm and listening.
The relative importance given to different criteria or sections of an assessment, expressed in marks or percentages. A weighting is a teaching decision that signals what matters most.

A learner’s readiness to enter into communication in a second language at a particular time with particular people (MacIntyre et al. 1998). It is influenced by confidence, anxiety and the classroom climate.
A base word together with its inflected and derived forms, such as help, helps, helped, helpful and helpless (Bauer and Nation 1993). Word families are often used to count vocabulary size.
All that is involved in knowing a word, including its form, meaning, grammar, collocations, register and use (Nation 2013). Knowing a word is gradual and multidimensional, not all-or-nothing.
The emphasis given to one syllable in a word, such as PHOtograph, phoTOgraphy and photoGRAPHic. Misplaced stress can affect intelligibility more than individual sounds.

The varieties of English used around the world, such as Indian, Nigerian and Singaporean English, each seen as legitimate with its own norms. The concept is closely associated with Kachru’s Three Circles model.
Learners of primary school age, roughly 5 to 12, who learn through activity, play and routine, have short attention spans and need concrete, meaningful tasks.

The gap between what a learner can do alone and what they can do with support from a teacher or more capable peer (Vygotsky 1978). Teaching aimed within this zone, with scaffolding, promotes development.
